scenario_meta.title: Operation Midnight Cipher
scenario_meta.subtitle: Enterprise Ransomware & Data Exfiltration
objectives: Blunt the Medicare-themed spear-phishing campaign before it lands.
Contain compromised credentials without destroying evidence.
Make a defensible ransom decision with the CEO and counsel.
Leave no adversary persistence behind during recovery.
Give the Board recommendations that map to the controls that failed.

injects.title: Threat Intel Bulletin
injects.story: MS-ISAC issues a bulletin: APT-SHADOW is targeting healthcare with Medicare-themed spear-phishing. Three regional hospitals are already compromised. Your CISO calls an emergency briefing. Your email gateway historically bypasses spear-phishing at a 23% rate. You are IR Team Lead. What is your first move?

mitre.description: APT-SHADOW registered cms-medicare-billing[.]net 30 days prior to launching the campaign.

choices.text: Push emergency YARA/Sigma rules to SIEM for known IOCs, brief SOC, notify department heads about Medicare-themed phishing themes.
choices.feedback: EXCELLENT. Proactive IOC distribution and user awareness are textbook NIST SP 800-61 r2 §3.1 preparation controls. You gain early detection advantage.

choices.text: Forward bulletin to IT helpdesk and increase email filtering sensitivity across the board.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL. Blunt filter tuning causes false positives. You missed targeted detection logic and user awareness opportunities.

choices.text: Mark as low priority — existing controls are robust. Schedule a quarterly review.
choices.feedback: CRITICAL FAILURE. Dismissing an active targeted threat bulletin violates HIPAA §164.308(a)(1) and NIST CSF Identify function. This will be scrutinized in any post-incident legal review.

injects.title: Credential Harvested
injects.story: Accounts Payable employee Margaret Chen clicked a Medicare-update link and entered her AD credentials on cms-medicare-billing[.]net before calling the helpdesk. Proxy logs show a 47-second connection. The domain passed SPF checks. What do you do?

story_variants.optimal: Your Sigma rule fires within minutes: Accounts Payable employee Margaret Chen clicked a Medicare-update link and entered her AD credentials on cms-medicare-billing[.]net. Because department heads were briefed, she calls the helpdesk immediately. Proxy logs show a 47-second connection. The domain passed SPF checks. What do you do?
story_variants.neutral: The tightened filters quarantined 400 legitimate emails overnight — and still let the lure through. Accounts Payable employee Margaret Chen clicked a Medicare-update link and entered her AD credentials on cms-medicare-billing[.]net. She only mentions it to the helpdesk two hours later while asking about a missing invoice. Proxy logs show a 47-second connection. The domain passed SPF checks. What do you do?
story_variants.detrimental: Nobody was watching for it. Accounts Payable employee Margaret Chen clicked a Medicare-update link and entered her AD credentials on cms-medicare-billing[.]net. The helpdesk only learns of it a day later, when her account starts triggering failed-logon alerts on a finance server. Proxy logs show a 47-second connection. The domain passed SPF checks. What do you do?

mitre.description: Targeted spear-phishing with credential-harvesting link using a lookalike domain that bypassed SPF validation.

choices.text: Disable Margaret's AD account, force Accounts Payable password resets, block the domain at the firewall, preserve all logs as evidence, escalate to Tier 2.
choices.feedback: EXCELLENT. Account lockout, blast-radius assessment, IOC blocking, and evidence preservation per NIST SP 800-61 r2 §3.2. HIPAA breach clock properly noted.

choices.text: Ask Margaret to change her password via the IT portal and send a phishing awareness email to staff.
choices.feedback: INADEQUATE. A password change doesn't stop already-harvested credentials. No IOC blocking, no evidence preservation, blast radius unscoped.

choices.text: Wait 24 hours to gather more evidence before acting to avoid business disruption.
choices.feedback: CRITICAL FAILURE. 24 hours with a compromised credential is catastrophic. The HIPAA breach determination clock starts now regardless of inaction.

injects.title: Ransomware Detonates
injects.story: Despite partial containment, the attacker pre-deployed ransomware via GPO to 14 workstations. Files encrypted with .SHADOWCRYPT extension. Ransom note demands 45 BTC (~$2.7M). Tested backups from 3 days ago exist. CEO asks: should we pay?

story_variants.optimal: Your rapid lockout limited the attacker's window, but a GPO change pushed in the first hour was missed: ransomware detonates on 14 workstations. Files are encrypted with the .SHADOWCRYPT extension. The ransom note demands 45 BTC (~$2.7M). Tested backups from 3 days ago exist, and your evidence preservation means the intrusion timeline is intact. The CEO asks: should we pay?
story_variants.neutral: The password change did not end the session the attacker already held. Ransomware pushed via GPO detonates on 14 workstations and two file servers. Files are encrypted with the .SHADOWCRYPT extension. The ransom note demands 45 BTC (~$2.7M). Tested backups from 3 days ago exist. The CEO asks: should we pay?
story_variants.detrimental: Twenty-four hours of unhindered access was all it took. Ransomware deployed via GPO detonates across 14 workstations, the file servers, and the imaging archive. Files are encrypted with the .SHADOWCRYPT extension. The ransom note demands 45 BTC (~$2.7M) and claims patient records were taken first. Tested backups from 3 days ago exist. The CEO asks: should we pay?

mitre.description: Ransomware deployed via GPO for mass encryption — classic big-game hunting technique.

choices.text: Recommend against payment. Invoke backup recovery plan, notify FBI and CISA, rebuild from gold images, document for cyber insurance.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Paying may violate OFAC if actor is SDN-listed. FBI notification enables attribution. Backups are the right recovery path. Board transparency required under HIPAA.

choices.text: Pay partial ransom to restore critical patient systems while restoring others from backup.
choices.feedback: HIGH RISK. Partial payment may violate OFAC, funds criminals, and provides no decryption guarantee.

choices.text: Pay the full ransom immediately and keep it quiet to restore operations fast.
choices.feedback: CATASTROPHIC. Potential OFAC sanctions violation. Keeping it quiet violates HIPAA mandatory disclosure, SEC rules, and state breach laws.

injects.title: Backdoor Discovered During Rebuild
injects.story: During reimaging, EDR detects a scheduled task 'MicrosoftEdgeUpdateCore' on a server missed in the initial scope — running Base64-encoded PowerShell every 4 hours, beaconing to a Tor exit node. This server was not on the affected list.

story_variants.optimal: Recovery from backups is under way and the FBI has shared IOCs from other victims. During reimaging, EDR detects a scheduled task 'MicrosoftEdgeUpdateCore' on a server missed in the initial scope — running Base64-encoded PowerShell every 4 hours, beaconing to a Tor exit node. This server was not on the affected list.
story_variants.neutral: The partial payment bought a decryptor that works on roughly half the files; the rest are being restored from backup. During reimaging, EDR detects a scheduled task 'MicrosoftEdgeUpdateCore' on a server missed in the initial scope — running Base64-encoded PowerShell every 4 hours, beaconing to a Tor exit node. This server was not on the affected list.
story_variants.detrimental: The ransom was paid and kept quiet; the decryptor is slow and corrupts some files, so IT is quietly rebuilding anyway. During reimaging, EDR detects a scheduled task 'MicrosoftEdgeUpdateCore' on a server missed in the initial scope — running Base64-encoded PowerShell every 4 hours, beaconing to a Tor exit node. This server was not on the affected list, and no one has yet asked whether the payment was screened against sanctions lists.

mitre.description: Attacker created a masqueraded scheduled task to maintain C2 access and survive recovery efforts.

choices.text: Hunt for the scheduled task name across ALL endpoints via EDR. Isolate any hits, capture forensic images, eradicate. Block the C2 IP. Delay recovery-complete declaration.
choices.feedback: EXCELLENT. Enterprise-wide hunting before declaring recovery is essential. Premature recovery declaration is a leading cause of re-infection in ransomware incidents.

choices.text: Delete the scheduled task on this one server and reimage it. Continue recovery.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT SCOPE. Treating a persistence mechanism as isolated risks missing attacker footholds on other systems, guaranteeing re-compromise.

choices.text: Declare recovery complete — this is likely a false positive from a legitimate update tool.
choices.feedback: FAILURE. An active C2 beacon is not a false positive. Declaring recovery with a confirmed live backdoor in environment guarantees re-compromise.

injects.title: Post-Incident Review
injects.story: Three weeks post-incident. 47,000 PHI records confirmed exfiltrated. HHS OCR notification submitted. FBI investigation opened. Cyber insurance requires demonstrating reasonable controls. CISO needs PIR recommendations for the Board.

story_variants.optimal: Three weeks post-incident. The fleet-wide hunt found the scheduled task on two more servers; all were isolated and forensically imaged. 47,000 PHI records confirmed exfiltrated. HHS OCR notification submitted. FBI investigation opened. Cyber insurance requires demonstrating reasonable controls. The CISO needs PIR recommendations for the Board.
story_variants.neutral: Three weeks post-incident. The single server was reimaged, but a second beacon was found last week on a host nobody checked, and the investigation has reopened. 47,000 PHI records confirmed exfiltrated. HHS OCR notification submitted. FBI investigation opened. Cyber insurance requires demonstrating reasonable controls. The CISO needs PIR recommendations for the Board.
story_variants.detrimental: Three weeks post-incident. Recovery was declared complete — and the attacker returned through the 'false positive' scheduled task nine days later, forcing a second shutdown. 47,000 PHI records confirmed exfiltrated. HHS OCR notification submitted. FBI investigation opened. Cyber insurance is questioning coverage. The CISO needs PIR recommendations for the Board.

mitre.description: Systematic review of control failures and required improvements across people, process, and technology.

choices.text: Recommend: FIDO2 MFA for remote access, PAWs for privileged accounts, LSASS protection (RunAsPPL), CASB for cloud egress, quarterly tabletops, NIST CSF 2.0 gap mapping, Board briefing, updated Risk Register.
choices.feedback: EXEMPLARY. Every exploited vector addressed with specific controls. FIDO2 defeats credential phishing. PAWs limit exposure. RunAsPPL defeats credential dumping. CASB prevents cloud exfiltration.

choices.text: Recommend mandatory phishing training for all staff and a penetration test within 6 months.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. Training and pentests are necessary but don't address specific technical gaps. An OCR auditor will cite lack of technical remediation.

choices.text: Recommend purchasing higher cyber insurance coverage and updating the IRP policy document.
choices.feedback: GOVERNANCE FAILURE. Insurance transfers risk, it doesn't reduce it. Policy documents without technical controls is security theater.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Trusted Betrayal
scenario_meta.subtitle: Malicious Insider Data Theft

injects.title: HR Escalation Received
injects.story: HR notifies Security: Senior Developer Marcus Webb was passed over for promotion and submitted resignation effective in 30 days. He has become increasingly hostile. Your DLP is not tuned for insider scenarios and no User Behavior Analytics (UBA) is deployed. What is your first action?

mitre.description: Insiders leverage pre-existing legitimate access. The preparation phase must detect and limit access before exfiltration begins.

choices.text: Classify Marcus as high-risk. Covertly audit his recent data access, tune DLP for his accounts, review AD group memberships, coordinate with HR on offboarding timeline.
choices.feedback: EXCELLENT. Proactive access scoping and DLP tuning for a known at-risk user is textbook insider threat management per NIST SP 800-53 PS-4 and CISA Insider Threat guidance. Legally permissible on corporate assets.

choices.text: Do nothing yet — the employee hasn't done anything wrong. Wait for evidence.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. Insider threat programs exist precisely for proactive, lawful monitoring of high-risk individuals. Waiting means waiting until after data is already exfiltrated.

choices.text: Immediately revoke all of Marcus's access and lock his accounts as a precaution.
choices.feedback: OVERCORRECTION. Immediate revocation without HR/Legal alignment may constitute wrongful termination grounds, violate employment contracts, and alert the insider to your monitoring — potentially accelerating exfiltration.

injects.title: Anomalous Data Access Detected
injects.story: DLP alert: Marcus accessed 3,400 customer financial records — databases outside his normal development scope — over three evenings this week, 9 PM–11 PM each night. He zipped the files and emailed them to a personal Gmail account. The email was intercepted by DLP before delivery. What do you do?

mitre.description: Insider collected sensitive data beyond operational need and prepared it for exfiltration via personal email.

choices.text: Preserve the intercepted email as evidence (do not delete). Engage Legal and HR immediately. Expand covert monitoring. Document chain of custody. Do not alert Marcus yet.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Evidence preservation and chain of custody are essential for prosecution. Covert monitoring while building the legal case is standard practice. Premature confrontation destroys the investigation.

choices.text: Block Marcus's Gmail access and send him a policy reminder about personal email use.
choices.feedback: INADEQUATE. Blocking Gmail without preserving evidence or involving Legal may compromise admissibility. A policy reminder immediately alerts the insider to your knowledge.

choices.text: Confront Marcus directly and ask him to explain the data access.
choices.feedback: SERIOUS ERROR. Direct confrontation destroys covert investigation, likely causes evidence destruction, and prejudices any legal case. Never confront until Legal authorizes it.

injects.title: USB Exfiltration Confirmed
injects.story: DLP and endpoint agents show Marcus plugged a USB drive into his workstation at 10:44 PM last night — outside business hours. 2.1 GB transferred. He called in sick this morning. Legal has now authorized account suspension. What is your containment sequence?

mitre.description: Insider exfiltrated data via physical USB, bypassing all network DLP controls entirely.

choices.text: Suspend all Marcus's accounts and remote access. Preserve his workstation as forensic evidence — do NOT wipe it. Secure his physical workspace. Coordinate termination with HR and a Law Enforcement referral.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Synchronized suspension, forensic preservation (not wiping!), physical security, and LE referral is the proper sequence. Wiping the workstation before forensic imaging destroys your criminal case.

choices.text: Suspend his accounts and remotely wipe his workstation to prevent further data access.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL. Account suspension is correct but remote wipe destroys forensic evidence needed for prosecution. This is a serious evidence preservation failure.

choices.text: Wait for Marcus to return from sick leave to conduct an in-person interview before acting.
choices.feedback: FAILURE. Waiting gives Marcus time to destroy USB evidence and further exfiltrate data remotely. Accounts must be suspended immediately upon Legal authorization.

injects.title: Backdoor Account Discovered
injects.story: Forensic analysis of Marcus's workstation reveals he created a local administrator account 'svc_monitor99' on a production server two weeks ago — a backdoor for post-termination access. Review authentication logs: was this account used after his suspension?

mitre.description: Insider pre-positioned a backdoor local account on production servers to maintain access after termination.

choices.text: Disable svc_monitor99, audit ALL local admin accounts across the enterprise for similar backdoors, review auth logs for post-suspension usage, and conduct full privilege audit of production servers.
choices.feedback: EXCELLENT. Enterprise-wide local account auditing is essential — insiders commonly create backdoors on multiple systems. Auth log review confirms whether post-suspension access occurred, affecting legal charges.

choices.text: Disable svc_monitor99 and change passwords on all accounts on that specific server.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT SCOPE. You've fixed one server. Insider threat actors create multiple persistence mechanisms across multiple systems. Enterprise-wide audit is required.

choices.text: Delete the account and move on — the insider is terminated and can't get back in.
choices.feedback: FALSE CONFIDENCE. Deleting without logging post-suspension access destroys evidence for unauthorized access charges under 18 U.S.C. §1030. 'Can't get back in' is an untested assumption without an enterprise-wide audit.

injects.title: Regulatory Notification Decision
injects.story: The 3,400 exfiltrated customer financial records include PII covered under GLBA and state breach notification laws. Legal confirms this is a reportable breach. Law enforcement has all evidence. What is your notification strategy?

mitre.description: GLBA Safeguards Rule and state breach statutes create mandatory notification obligations for financial services data theft.

choices.text: Notify affected customers per state breach laws (30–60 days). File GLBA-required notification with your primary federal regulator (OCC/FDIC). Coordinate timing with Law Enforcement to avoid prejudicing the investigation.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY REQUIRED AND CORRECT. GLBA Safeguards Rule requires notifying your federal regulator within 30 days. State laws require customer notification. LE coordination on timing is critical to avoid tipping off accomplices.

choices.text: Wait for the criminal case to conclude before notifying customers to avoid prejudicing the trial.
choices.feedback: COMPLIANCE FAILURE. Criminal proceedings do not pause regulatory notification obligations. Delaying customer notification beyond statutory deadlines creates independent regulatory liability.

choices.text: Don't notify anyone externally — the incident is contained and public disclosure will damage the firm's reputation.
choices.feedback: ILLEGAL. Deliberate suppression of a reportable breach violates GLBA, state breach laws, and potentially SEC Rule 10b-5. This is the definition of a cover-up and creates massive personal liability for executives.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Poisoned Update
scenario_meta.subtitle: Software Supply Chain Compromise

injects.title: Overdue Vendor Assessment
injects.story: Your CI/CD tool vendor 'BuildMaster Pro' has an overdue security questionnaire (60 days). A new CISA advisory warns that CI/CD tools in the defense sector are being targeted by nation-state actors. Your org has 200 developers using this tool. What is your priority action?

mitre.description: Nation-state actors pre-position by compromising trusted vendor infrastructure before targeting downstream organizations.

choices.text: Escalate as critical: request BuildMaster Pro's SOC 2 Type II report and software signing practices, implement network monitoring on BuildMaster traffic, and demand questionnaire completion within 48 hours.
choices.feedback: EXCELLENT. Software signing verification, SOC 2 review, and behavioral monitoring are exactly the supply chain controls recommended by NIST SP 800-161r1 and CISA Supply Chain Risk Management Guidance.

choices.text: Send a reminder email and extend the deadline by 30 days.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. A 60-day overdue questionnaire during an active advisory is a red flag, not an administrative inconvenience. Extensions without escalation demonstrate inadequate TPRM governance.

choices.text: No action — BuildMaster Pro is a well-known vendor; they wouldn't be compromised.
choices.feedback: DANGEROUS ASSUMPTION. SolarWinds, Kaseya, and 3CX were all well-known vendors. Brand recognition is not a security control. This is precisely the attitude nation-state supply chain attackers exploit.

injects.title: Trojanized Update Deployed
injects.story: BuildMaster Pro released version 4.2.1 overnight. Automated systems applied it to all 200 developer workstations this morning. By 10 AM, EDR shows BuildMaster spawning PowerShell and beaconing to an unknown IP on port 443. CISA issues an emergency alert: BuildMaster 4.2.1 is confirmed trojanized.

mitre.technique: Supply Chain Compromise: Software Supply Chain
mitre.description: Attacker compromised the vendor's build pipeline and inserted a backdoor into a legitimate signed software update.

choices.text: Halt all BuildMaster processes enterprise-wide. Isolate all affected developer workstations. Block the beacon IP/domain at the perimeter. Treat all 200 machines as compromised. Notify CISA per CIRCIA and engage your IR retainer.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Enterprise-wide containment of a confirmed trojanized tool is required. CIRCIA reporting for defense critical infrastructure is mandatory. The active beacon indicates C2 is already established.

choices.text: Roll back BuildMaster to the previous version and monitor for 48 hours.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL. Rollback is necessary but insufficient — the malicious update may have already executed payloads. Monitoring for 48 hours allows an active attacker continued dwell time.

choices.text: Wait for the vendor to release a patch before taking action to avoid disrupting developer productivity.
choices.feedback: UNACCEPTABLE. An active C2 beacon from a confirmed trojanized tool cannot wait for a vendor patch. Every minute allows the nation-state actor to pivot, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate source code.

injects.title: Source Code Repository Cloned
injects.story: Forensics shows the trojanized BuildMaster accessed your GitHub Enterprise instance and cloned 14 private repositories containing classified project source code and cryptographic key material. The clone occurred 6 hours before detection. What is your priority containment action?

mitre.description: Attacker used compromised CI/CD credentials to access and exfiltrate private source code repositories containing secrets.

choices.text: Immediately rotate all GitHub Enterprise tokens, SSH keys, and service account credentials. Revoke and regenerate all cryptographic keys exposed in the repositories. Engage CISA and DCSA given the defense contract context.
choices.feedback: CRITICAL AND CORRECT. Any cryptographic key or secret in a cloned repository must be treated as permanently compromised — rotation cannot wait. DCSA notification may be required under CMMC and defense contract obligations.

choices.text: Revoke the specific BuildMaster service account token used for the clone.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. Revoking one token doesn't address credentials cloned from repo contents, API keys embedded in code, or the full blast radius of 14 compromised repositories.

choices.text: Set the repositories to private and consider the incident contained.
choices.feedback: FUNDAMENTALLY WRONG. The repositories were already cloned — the data is in the attacker's hands. Setting repos to private has no retroactive effect on data already exfiltrated.

injects.title: Golden Ticket Attack Confirmed
injects.story: Memory forensics reveals Mimikatz was executed and the KRBTGT hash was extracted from a domain controller the attacker pivoted to. A Golden Ticket was forged — giving the attacker domain-level Kerberos access valid for 10 years. How do you remediate?

mitre.technique: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket
mitre.description: Attacker forged a Kerberos ticket using the stolen KRBTGT hash, granting persistent domain-level access that survives standard password changes.

choices.text: Reset the KRBTGT account password TWICE with propagation time between resets — required to fully invalidate all existing tickets. Force re-authentication of all domain accounts. Implement Protected Users security group for all privileged accounts.
choices.feedback: TECHNICALLY CORRECT. KRBTGT must be reset twice — the previous hash is cached and a single reset is insufficient. This is per Microsoft guidance. Protected Users group prevents Kerberos delegation abuse going forward.

choices.text: Reset the KRBTGT password once and force all users to reset their own passwords.
choices.feedback: INCOMPLETE. A single KRBTGT reset does NOT fully invalidate Golden Tickets because the previous hash is cached. Two resets with propagation delay between them is the required remediation per Microsoft guidance.

choices.text: Reimage all affected developer workstations — this will eliminate the attacker's access.
choices.feedback: MISUNDERSTANDING THE ATTACK. A Golden Ticket is a domain-level persistence mechanism — it lives in Kerberos infrastructure, not on workstations. Reimaging endpoints has no effect on forged domain tickets.

injects.title: Federal Disclosure Obligations
injects.story: Your organization holds federal contracts. Cloned repositories contained CUI (Controlled Unclassified Information) and ITAR-controlled technical data. DFARS 252.204-7012 and CMMC Level 2 obligations apply. The DCSA contracting officer is calling. What is your response?

mitre.description: Defense contractors have mandatory 72-hour cyber incident reporting under DFARS and must preserve evidence for DoD assessment.

choices.text: Report to DoD via the DIBNet portal within 72 hours per DFARS 252.204-7012. Preserve all forensic media. Provide the contracting officer a preliminary impact assessment. Engage a CMMC C3PAO. Submit malware samples to US-CERT.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY REQUIRED AND CORRECT. DFARS mandates 72-hour written reporting — missing this deadline voids contract protections and may constitute a False Claims Act violation. All steps are mandatory.

choices.text: Notify the contracting officer verbally and promise a written report within 30 days.
choices.feedback: NON-COMPLIANT. DFARS requires written reporting via DIBNet within 72 hours. A verbal notification and 30-day delay violates the contractual requirement and exposes the org to FCA liability.

choices.text: Classify the breach scope as minimal and don't report to avoid contract termination risk.
choices.feedback: ILLEGAL. Deliberate underreporting of a CUI/ITAR breach to a federal contracting officer constitutes a False Claims Act violation and potentially obstruction. Criminal referral is a likely outcome.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Open Bucket
scenario_meta.subtitle: AWS S3 Cloud Misconfiguration Data Exposure

injects.title: Public S3 Bucket Flagged
injects.story: A quarterly cloud security assessment flags 3 S3 buckets with 's3:GetObject' granted to '*' (public). One contains customer PII. Engineering says a fix requires a 2-sprint effort. The finding is rated Medium. What is your response?

mitre.description: Attackers use automated scanners to enumerate public cloud storage. Misconfigured S3 buckets are discovered within hours of exposure.

choices.text: Reclassify as CRITICAL. Apply AWS account-level Block Public Access as an emergency compensating control today while engineering schedules the proper IAM fix.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. AWS Block Public Access is a one-click emergency control. Reclassifying severity and applying compensating controls while a sprint is scheduled is the right risk management approach per GDPR data protection by design.

choices.text: Accept the risk for one sprint cycle (2 weeks) and add to the risk register.
choices.feedback: INADEQUATE. Public S3 buckets with customer PII can be discovered and exfiltrated within hours. A 2-week acceptance window violates GDPR's data protection by design principle.

choices.text: Close the finding — these buckets need to be public for the CDN to function.
choices.feedback: TECHNICAL MISUNDERSTANDING. CDN distributions access S3 via Origin Access Control (OAC), not public bucket policies. Closing this finding without verification is a serious governance failure.

injects.title: Breach Detected via Customer Tweet
injects.story: A customer tweets their data appeared on a breach site. SIEM shows 340,000 API calls to 'prod-customer-backup-2023' from a single IP over 72 hours. The bucket contains names, emails, addresses, and hashed passwords for 2.3M users. NetFlow confirms 2.3 GB exfiltrated.

mitre.description: Attacker used automated tooling to enumerate and bulk-download all objects from a publicly accessible S3 bucket over 72 hours.

choices.text: Enable S3 Block Public Access immediately. Preserve all S3 access logs and CloudTrail events as evidence. Scope exact data contents for breach notification. Engage Legal for GDPR/CCPA assessment. Prepare customer advisory.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. GDPR Article 33 requires DPA notification within 72 hours of discovery — that clock is now running. Evidence preservation and legal assessment must happen in parallel with technical remediation.

choices.text: Make the bucket private and wait to see if any customers report fraud before deciding on notification.
choices.feedback: NON-COMPLIANT. GDPR requires proactive DPA notification within 72 hours — not after waiting for evidence of harm. 'Wait and see' violates both GDPR and CCPA.

choices.text: Make the bucket private and delete the access logs to prevent further analysis of the exposure scope.
choices.feedback: ILLEGAL. Deleting access logs is destruction of evidence and constitutes obstruction. This single action transforms a data breach fine into potential criminal charges against individuals.

injects.title: Credential Stuffing Wave Begins
injects.story: Cracked passwords from the exposed bucket are being used in a credential stuffing attack against your login portal. 14,000 accounts accessed in 6 hours. Account takeover rate is accelerating. Your WAF is detecting the volume spike.

mitre.description: Attacker used cracked credentials from the breach to conduct credential stuffing, gaining access to legitimate customer accounts at scale.

choices.text: Enable WAF rate limiting on the login endpoint. Force a password reset for all 2.3M exposed accounts. Implement temporary CAPTCHA. Notify customers not to reuse passwords elsewhere. Alert the fraud team.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Forced enterprise-wide password reset for all exposed accounts, WAF throttling, and proactive customer communication stops the ATO wave and demonstrates duty of care for regulatory review.

choices.text: Block the attacking IP ranges at the WAF and monitor login rates.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. IP blocking is easily bypassed via residential proxies common in credential stuffing. The compromised credential problem must be fixed, not just the IP surface.

choices.text: Take the login portal offline to stop account takeovers.
choices.feedback: OVERCORRECTION. Taking the portal offline creates a self-inflicted DoS and revenue loss without addressing the compromised credentials. Surgical forced password resets protect accounts while maintaining availability.

injects.title: IAM Over-Privilege Root Cause
injects.story: Post-incident IAM audit: 47 IAM users have AdministratorAccess attached. No SCPs exist at the AWS Organizations level. The public bucket policy was created by a developer with admin-level credentials. No guardrails prevented it. What is your architectural remediation?

mitre.description: Excessive IAM privilege allowed developers to misconfigure production resources without any preventive guardrails at the organization layer.

choices.text: Implement AWS Organizations SCPs denying 's3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock false'. Migrate all developers to least-privilege roles. Deploy IAM Access Analyzer and AWS Config rules for compliance detection.
choices.feedback: ARCHITECTURAL EXCELLENCE. SCPs are enforced at the org level — even admin users cannot override them. IAM Access Analyzer and Config create detective layers. This is cloud security defense-in-depth per the AWS Well-Architected Framework.

choices.text: Remove AdministratorAccess from the specific developer who created the misconfiguration.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT SCOPE. 47 other users still have AdministratorAccess. Fixing one person without fixing the systemic over-privilege means the same misconfiguration can happen again tomorrow.

choices.text: Require developers to document their rationale when creating S3 buckets going forward.
choices.feedback: SECURITY THEATER. Documentation is an administrative control. It does not prevent misconfiguration. Technical preventive controls — SCPs and IAM boundaries — are required. Paperwork is not a substitute.

injects.title: GDPR Regulatory Investigation
injects.story: GDPR's supervisory authority is investigating. They've requested your timeline — including when the quarterly assessment flagged the bucket (before breach) and your notification timeline. Maximum fine is 4% of global annual revenue (~$8M). Legal needs your cooperation strategy.

mitre.description: GDPR Article 83 fine assessment explicitly considers organizational cooperation and remediation as mitigating factors.

choices.text: Recommend full transparency: provide the complete timeline including the pre-existing finding, demonstrate proactive remediation (SCPs, IAM changes), show implemented controls, and provide a detailed remediation plan. Cooperation demonstrably reduces GDPR fines.
choices.feedback: STRATEGICALLY CORRECT. GDPR Article 83(2) explicitly lists organizational cooperation and remediation as mitigating factors. Regulators consistently reduce fines for organizations that demonstrate good faith transparency.

choices.text: Provide minimum required documentation and have Legal handle all DPA communications.
choices.feedback: SUBOPTIMAL. A purely defensive posture with a GDPR regulator often results in maximum fine calculations. Regulators have broad investigative powers — minimalism rarely reduces exposure.

choices.text: Argue to the DPA that the quarterly assessment finding was a different issue unrelated to the breach.
choices.feedback: COUNTER-PRODUCTIVE. Documentary evidence proves the risk was identified and not remediated. Arguing otherwise will be viewed by the DPA as an aggravating factor, increasing the likely fine.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Flood Wall
scenario_meta.subtitle: Multi-Vector DDoS Extortion Attack

injects.title: Ransom Demand Received
injects.story: You receive an email: 'Pay 5 BTC by Friday or we take your platform offline during your largest gaming event of the year (est. 2M concurrent users).' Attached is a proof-of-concept 4-minute traffic spike from last night. What is your response?

mitre.description: Threat actor demonstrates DDoS capability with a proof-of-concept attack and demands payment to forestall a full attack during a high-value business event.

choices.text: Do not pay. Immediately engage your DDoS mitigation provider for emergency scrubbing capacity, notify your ISP for upstream filtering, pre-position rate limiting and anycast failover, brief engineering teams on runbooks, and report the extortion to the FBI.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Paying DDoS extortion invites repeat demands — groups routinely attack anyway after payment. Proactive mitigation and FBI reporting is the standard response. FBI IC3 is the correct reporting channel.

choices.text: Forward to Legal and take no technical action pending their guidance.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. Legal guidance is needed but technical preparation cannot wait. DDoS mitigation capacity must be engaged immediately — the attack window is days away.

choices.text: Pay the 5 BTC to protect the event revenue.
choices.feedback: HIGH RISK. Payment funds criminal enterprise, provides no guarantee of non-attack, invites future demands, and may violate OFAC sanctions. The FBI advises against paying extortion demands.

injects.title: Multi-Vector Attack Begins
injects.story: The attack starts: 480 Gbps volumetric UDP flood plus an application-layer HTTP GET flood targeting the login API. Your scrubbing center absorbs the volumetric traffic but the L7 attack is bypassing it. 45,000 players disconnecting per minute.

mitre.technique: Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
mitre.description: Multi-vector attack combining L3/L4 volumetric UDP amplification with L7 HTTP flood to defeat single-layer mitigation strategies.

choices.text: Engage WAF rate limiting on the login API, enable CAPTCHA for new connections, implement IP reputation blocking for botnet CIDRs, and push L7 mitigations via CDN provider. Triage which game servers to protect vs. gracefully shed.
choices.feedback: TECHNICALLY CORRECT. Multi-vector DDoS requires layer-appropriate mitigations. L3/L4 scrubbing handles volumetric; WAF + rate limiting + CAPTCHA handles L7. Triage decisions protect core revenue-generating services.

choices.text: Shut down the entire platform to prevent further reputational damage from lag.
choices.feedback: OVERCORRECTION. A self-inflicted total outage achieves the attacker's goal and maximizes revenue loss. Surgical mitigation to protect critical services is always preferable to full shutdown.

choices.text: Block all traffic from geographic regions with high attack traffic volumes.
choices.feedback: GEO-BLOCKING FAILURE. Botnets use globally distributed infected hosts — geo-blocking causes massive false positives (legitimate players blocked) while the attacker simply pivots to botnet nodes in other regions.

injects.title: Origin IP Bypass Discovered
injects.story: Analysis shows the L7 attack is hitting your origin servers directly — the attacker enumerated your origin IP via historical DNS records and a 2019 SSL certificate transparency log. The CDN is being bypassed. Scrubbing can't help with direct-to-origin traffic.

mitre.description: Attacker identified the origin IP behind the CDN via historical DNS records and certificate transparency logs, enabling direct attacks that bypass CDN DDoS protection.

choices.text: Change origin server IP addresses. Update CDN configuration. Implement network ACLs on origin to only accept traffic from CDN CIDR ranges. Audit all DNS records and purge historical origin IP exposure.
choices.feedback: ARCHITECTURALLY CORRECT. IP rotation breaks the direct attack path. CDN CIDR allowlisting prevents future bypass. DNS record cleanup prevents re-discovery. This is the correct CDN hardening sequence.

choices.text: Add more origin servers to distribute the load.
choices.feedback: DOESN'T FIX THE PROBLEM. Adding servers is expensive and futile — the attacker can scale their botnet. The architectural flaw (exposed origin IP) must be fixed, not scaled around.

choices.text: Route origin traffic through a second CDN as an additional layer.
choices.feedback: WRONG SOLUTION. The origin IP is already known — adding another CDN layer doesn't hide an already-exposed IP. The origin IP must change and be locked to CDN-only traffic.

injects.title: Architecture Post-Mortem
injects.story: Attack subsided after 6 hours. Revenue loss: ~$400K. Post-incident review reveals: no DDoS runbook, no pre-contracted scrubbing, origin IP exposed in Shodan and cert transparency logs. Your CTO wants a priority remediation plan before the next event in 6 weeks.

mitre.description: Post-DDoS architecture review to implement preventive controls against future multi-vector attacks with documented runbooks.

choices.text: Pre-contract always-on DDoS scrubbing (not on-demand — too slow to activate). Create and test DDoS runbooks with decision trees per attack vector. Implement BGP anycast routing. Harden CDN/origin architecture with CIDR allowlisting. Conduct a dedicated DDoS threat model.
choices.feedback: MATURE RESILIENCE PLANNING. Always-on scrubbing has significantly lower activation latency than on-demand. Runbooks enable fast response without heroic engineering effort. Anycast and CDN hardening address the root causes identified in this incident.

choices.text: Purchase cyber insurance that covers DDoS revenue loss.
choices.feedback: RISK TRANSFER IS NOT RISK REDUCTION. Insurance doesn't prevent attacks or reduce their impact duration. Technical resilience controls must come first; insurance supplements them.

choices.text: Accept the risk — DDoS attacks are a cost of doing business in gaming.
choices.feedback: GOVERNANCE FAILURE. A documented $400K loss event with a clear root cause and available technical remediation cannot be accepted without remediation. Risk acceptance without treatment is not defensible governance.

injects.title: Community Crisis Response
injects.story: Community forums are erupting. Players demand compensation for the 6-hour disruption. Your Legal team confirms no contractual obligation exists, but notes ToS language around 'reasonable uptime.' PR warns that silence will cause long-term churn. What do you recommend?

mitre.description: Post-incident stakeholder management following service disruption — transparency and concrete remediation steps rebuild customer trust.

choices.text: Issue a transparent incident post-mortem explaining what happened (appropriately scoped), what you've fixed to prevent recurrence, and offer in-game compensation. Transparency combined with concrete remediation is the gold standard crisis response.
choices.feedback: EXCELLENT. Transparent post-mortems with concrete remediation commitments consistently result in better long-term customer retention than silence. Community trust is rebuilt through honesty.

choices.text: Post a brief 'we experienced technical difficulties' statement with a small in-game compensation item.
choices.feedback: MINIMAL. Vague language when the community knows it was an attack undermines trust. Appropriate transparency about the nature of the incident is generally better received.

choices.text: Say nothing — any acknowledgment could create legal liability for future attacks.
choices.feedback: COUNTERPRODUCTIVE. Silence in the face of a known, widely-discussed outage destroys community trust faster than any response. The legal rationale here is overstated — general DDoS transparency creates minimal legal exposure.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Silver Tongue
scenario_meta.subtitle: CEO Whaling / BEC Wire Fraud Attempt

injects.title: Lookalike Domain Registered
injects.story: Brand monitoring alerts: someone registered acme-corp-finance[.]com (your domain: acmecorp.com) 3 days ago. Valid SSL and MX record exist. No emails sent yet. OSINT shows your CFO recently posted on LinkedIn about 'a major acquisition in progress.' What do you do?

mitre.description: BEC actors register lookalike domains in advance of targeted whaling attacks, exploiting executive social media for business intelligence.

choices.text: Report the lookalike domain to the registrar for abuse takedown. Brief the CFO and CEO on likely BEC targeting. Implement DMARC p=reject on your domain. Establish an out-of-band phone verification protocol for all wire transfers exceeding $50K.
choices.feedback: PROACTIVE AND CORRECT. Registrar abuse reports often suspend domains within 48 hours. Out-of-band verification is the single most effective BEC countermeasure. DMARC prevents domain spoofing. All four actions are warranted.

choices.text: Monitor the domain for actual malicious activity before taking action.
choices.feedback: REACTIVE. BEC actors move fast — fraudulent wire requests often arrive within 24–72 hours of domain registration. Waiting for activity means waiting until fraud is already in motion.

choices.text: No action needed unless an actual attack occurs.
choices.feedback: MISSED OPPORTUNITY. Pre-attack intelligence is the most valuable intervention point. FBI IC3 reports $2.9B in annual BEC losses — acting on early indicators is the only reliable prevention mechanism.

injects.title: Fraudulent Wire Request Arrives
injects.story: CFO receives an email from 'CEO James Mitchell' at james.mitchell@acme-corp-finance[.]com while the real CEO is traveling: 'Wire $2.3M to our acquisition escrow today — extremely time sensitive, do not discuss with anyone.' The CFO flags it to Security. How do you respond?

mitre.description: BEC actor used a lookalike domain to impersonate the CEO, pressuring the CFO into an unauthorized wire transfer via urgency and authority cues.

choices.text: Confirm this is the lookalike domain — NOT the real CEO. Call the real CEO on a known personal mobile number to verify. Have the CFO reply that the request is 'being processed' to gather attacker intelligence. Alert the FBI IC3 and your bank's wire fraud team.
choices.feedback: EXCELLENT. Out-of-band phone verification immediately confirms fraud. Stringing along the attacker while engaging FBI and the bank creates a possibility of recovery if any funds moved. FBI IC3 reporting is critical for investigation.

choices.text: Reply to the email asking the 'CEO' for more details about the acquisition.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL. Buying time is good but email reply signals engagement to the attacker. The real CEO should be called immediately via an out-of-band channel — not engaged via the fraudulent email thread.

choices.text: Process the wire transfer — it appears to come from the CEO and the timing is urgent.
choices.feedback: CATASTROPHIC. $2.3M wired to a fraudulent escrow is rarely recoverable. FinCEN data shows less than 30% recovery even with immediate FBI intervention. Urgency + secrecy is the #1 BEC red flag taught in every awareness training.

injects.title: CFO Mailbox Compromised
injects.story: Investigation reveals the attacker had been reading the CFO's Microsoft 365 mailbox for 3 weeks via an AiTM phishing kit — explaining their perfect knowledge of the acquisition deal. The attacker has a valid authenticated session right now.

mitre.description: Attacker maintained persistent access to the CFO's email account via stolen session cookie, gathering M&A intelligence for a precisely tailored BEC attack.

choices.text: Revoke ALL active sessions for the CFO account (M365 'Sign out everywhere' + token revocation). Review all M365 audit logs for emails read, forwarding rules created, and data accessed. Notify M&A counsel and acquisition counterparties whose information may be exposed.
choices.feedback: THOROUGH AND CORRECT. Session token revocation (not just password reset) is required to evict an attacker using a stolen authenticated session cookie. Counterparty notification is critical — the attacker may target the other side of the acquisition.

choices.text: Reset the CFO's password and enable MFA on their account.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. Password reset doesn't invalidate a stolen session cookie — the attacker's browser session remains valid. Session revocation is the required action, not just credential rotation.

choices.text: No further action — the BEC attempt was caught before any money was sent.
choices.feedback: MAJOR OVERSIGHT. The CFO email compromise is an independent, ongoing security incident. The BEC attempt failing doesn't resolve the active credential compromise or the 3 weeks of intelligence the attacker gathered.

injects.title: Silent Forwarding Rules Found
injects.story: M365 audit logs reveal the attacker created inbox rules on the CFO account: all emails containing 'acquisition,' 'wire,' or 'escrow' are silently forwarded to a Gmail address and deleted from the inbox — a classic BEC persistence technique for maintaining intelligence access.

mitre.description: Attacker created silent inbox forwarding rules to maintain persistent email intelligence access while evading detection — a hallmark BEC persistence technique.

choices.text: Delete all malicious forwarding rules. Audit ALL executive mailboxes for similar rules — this is commonly deployed across multiple targets. Implement M365 Defender alerts for new inbox rules forwarding to external addresses. Block personal email forwarding via Exchange transport rules.
choices.feedback: COMPREHENSIVE. BEC actors routinely deploy forwarding rules on multiple executive targets. Enterprise-wide rule audit and preventive transport rules blocking external forwarding addresses the root cause organization-wide.

choices.text: Delete the forwarding rules on the CFO account only.
choices.feedback: INCOMPLETE SCOPE. You've fixed one mailbox. BEC actors systematically target CEO, COO, and Finance teams — the same rules likely exist on other executive mailboxes. Enterprise-wide audit is required.

choices.text: This was an isolated incident — no additional mailbox auditing needed.
choices.feedback: SCOPE UNDERESTIMATION. 'Isolated incident' is a dangerous assumption in BEC campaigns. Threat actors systematically target entire finance and executive teams. This posture guarantees missing additional compromised mailboxes.

injects.title: Board-Level Controls Recommendation
injects.story: The BEC attempt was foiled this time, but the CFO account was compromised for 3 weeks undetected and no out-of-band wire verification protocol existed. The Board wants concrete controls to prevent a repeat. What do you recommend?

mitre.description: Post-BEC control improvements addressing authentication, financial process controls, and executive-targeted detection.

choices.text: Recommend: FIDO2 MFA for all executive accounts, Conditional Access requiring compliant devices, M365 Defender alerts for suspicious inbox rule creation, mandatory out-of-band voice verification for all wire transfers >$25K, and executive-specific BEC simulations with whaling scenarios.
choices.feedback: COMPLETE BEC DEFENSE ARCHITECTURE. FIDO2 defeats AiTM phishing. Conditional Access limits attack surface. Defender rules detect forwarding rule creation in real time. Dual-channel wire verification is the most effective financial control. Executive simulations create visceral awareness.

choices.text: Send a BEC awareness email to all staff.
choices.feedback: NECESSARY BUT INSUFFICIENT. Awareness emails have low retention without reinforcement. Technical controls — MFA, Defender rules, wire verification protocols — are required alongside training.

choices.text: Purchase BEC-specific cyber insurance to cover future wire fraud losses.
choices.feedback: RISK TRANSFER ONLY. BEC insurance has strict conditions — many policies require demonstrating reasonable controls were in place. Without technical controls, claims may be denied. Prevention must come before insurance.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Silent Strike
scenario_meta.subtitle: Zero-Day Exploitation of Internet-Facing VPN Appliance

injects.title: KEV-Listed VPN Vulnerability
injects.story: Your VPN vendor releases an advisory: a critical unauthenticated RCE CVE exists in all versions prior to 9.1.4. Patch available now. CISA adds it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog same day. You have 47 appliances across 12 sites. What is your patching strategy?

mitre.description: KEV-listed vulnerability in internet-facing VPN appliance enables unauthenticated RCE — the highest priority patching scenario defined by CISA.

choices.text: Invoke emergency change management to patch within CISA's KEV timeline (72 hours). Stage patches starting with internet-facing appliances. Apply WAF rules as a compensating control. CRITICALLY: check all appliances for compromise indicators BEFORE patching.
choices.feedback: CORRECT PRIORITY. KEV-listed vulnerabilities are actively exploited — speed is paramount. Critically: checking for compromise before patching is essential because patching an already-compromised appliance doesn't remove attacker persistence.

choices.text: Schedule patching during the next maintenance window in 3 weeks per standard change management policy.
choices.feedback: INADEQUATE FOR KEV. Standard change windows do not apply to actively-exploited KEV vulnerabilities. CISA's mandate exists precisely to override standard patching timelines for the highest-risk vulnerabilities.

choices.text: Disable all VPN appliances entirely until patches are applied to eliminate risk.
choices.feedback: OVERCORRECTION. Disabling VPN across 12 critical infrastructure sites disrupts operations and remote SCADA monitoring. Staged patching with compensating controls maintains security without self-inflicted outage.

injects.title: Active Compromise IOCs Found
injects.story: While checking appliances pre-patch, Site 7's VPN appliance has artifacts consistent with exploitation: unexpected cron jobs, an unfamiliar binary '/tmp/.svc', and outbound connections to known APT infrastructure. Exploitation appears to have occurred 11 days ago.

mitre.description: APT exploited the zero-day to gain initial foothold on the VPN appliance, establishing persistence via cron jobs and a hidden binary before the patch was available.

choices.text: Isolate Site 7's VPN appliance immediately. Capture a forensic image BEFORE any changes. Treat all credentials that transited Site 7 VPN in the past 11 days as compromised and begin rotation. Notify CISA per CIRCIA given critical infrastructure context.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Isolation preserves evidence. 11 days of attacker access means all credentials transiting that VPN must be treated as compromised. CIRCIA reporting for critical infrastructure is mandatory. Forensic image before patching is essential.

choices.text: Patch the appliance immediately to evict the attacker.
choices.feedback: INCORRECT SEQUENCING. Patching without forensic imaging first destroys evidence. Patching also doesn't necessarily remove persistence mechanisms — eradication requires forensic-guided remediation, not just patching.

choices.text: Continue monitoring to gather more intelligence before acting.
choices.feedback: DANGEROUS. Nation-state actors pivot quickly once potentially detected. Monitoring an active APT on a VPN appliance connected to critical infrastructure OT networks is not a viable strategy.

injects.title: SCADA HMI Access Confirmed
injects.story: Memory forensics reveals the attacker pivoted to Site 7's OT network and accessed two SCADA HMIs controlling water treatment processes for 340,000 residents. The adversary had read/write access to HMI set-points for 8 days.

mitre.description: APT pivoted from compromised VPN appliance through the IT/OT boundary to access SCADA HMIs controlling water treatment critical infrastructure.

choices.text: Immediately isolate the OT network from IT/VPN at the Purdue Model boundary. Switch SCADA HMIs to manual/local control. Conduct emergency verification of all current process set-points against safe operating ranges. Notify EPA, CISA, and state utility regulator. Engage ICS-CERT.
choices.feedback: CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE RESPONSE CORRECT. OT/IT isolation is mandatory when APT access to SCADA is confirmed. Manual set-point verification protects public safety. Federal notifications are legally required under AWIA 2018 for water utility cyber incidents.

choices.text: Change SCADA HMI account passwords and increase monitoring.
choices.feedback: DANGEROUSLY INSUFFICIENT. Password changes don't close the network path from the VPN appliance to the OT network. The attacker may still have access. Manual set-point verification and OT isolation are required given public safety stakes.

choices.text: Continue operations — shutting down SCADA would disrupt water treatment for 340,000 residents.
choices.feedback: FALSE CHOICE. OT isolation doesn't shut down water treatment — SCADA switches to local manual control, which trained operators maintain safely. Operating SCADA with confirmed APT write access to set-points is the actual public safety risk.

injects.title: ICS Historian Data Exfiltrated
injects.story: Forensics confirms the APT exfiltrated 18 months of SCADA historian data: facility layouts, process parameters, equipment specifications, and treatment chemical dosing schedules. This operational intelligence could enable future targeted physical process attacks.

mitre.description: APT exfiltrated OT historian data providing operational intelligence to plan future targeted physical attacks on water treatment infrastructure.

choices.text: Classify historian data as permanently compromised intelligence. Brief DHS CISA, FBI, and WaterISAC on what was exfiltrated. Evaluate whether process parameters and chemical dosing schedules need operational changes. Implement historian network segmentation and access logging.
choices.feedback: SECTOR-APPROPRIATE. WaterISAC notification enables threat sharing with peer utilities. Treating exfiltrated operational data as permanently compromised and adjusting processes accordingly is the correct ICS-focused response to protect public safety.

choices.text: Document the exfiltration and continue normal operations.
choices.feedback: UNDERREACTION. Exfiltrated ICS historian data in APT hands constitutes a strategic intelligence loss enabling future physical attacks. Continuing without operational review and sector notification fails the public trust obligation of a utility.

choices.text: The historian data is operational, not sensitive — no special response needed.
choices.feedback: INCORRECT CLASSIFICATION. OT historian data containing process parameters and dosing schedules is precisely the intelligence needed to plan a targeted physical attack on critical infrastructure. This classification is dangerously wrong.

injects.title: AWIA 2018 Compliance Review
injects.story: America's Water Infrastructure Act (AWIA) 2018 requires water utilities to conduct cybersecurity risk assessments and certify compliance. Your last assessment was 3 years ago. The incident exposed significant gaps. EPA is inquiring about your AWIA certification status.

mitre.description: AWIA 2018 compliance and EPA regulatory response following a confirmed cyber intrusion into water utility OT systems.

choices.text: Commission an immediate AWIA-compliant cybersecurity risk assessment using the NIST CSF and WaterISAC guidelines. Engage EPA proactively with full disclosure. Develop a remediation plan with milestones. Brief the utility board and relevant elected officials.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Proactive EPA engagement with a committed remediation plan is far better than reactive enforcement. AWIA compliance is not optional — EPA has enforcement authority including fines and operational restrictions.

choices.text: Submit your 3-year-old risk assessment to EPA and note you are 'in the process of updating it.'
choices.feedback: NON-COMPLIANT. AWIA requires current assessments reflecting present risks. Submitting an assessment that predates a major compromise you are actively responding to is a material misrepresentation to a federal regulator.

choices.text: Do not respond to EPA's inquiry pending extended legal review.
choices.feedback: REGULATORY ESCALATION. Non-response to EPA inquiries about mandatory compliance certifications will be interpreted as non-compliance and may trigger formal enforcement proceedings. Legal review and regulatory response must happen in parallel.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Trojan Badge
scenario_meta.subtitle: Physical Security Breach Enabling Cyber Network Access

injects.title: Tailgating Pattern Detected
injects.story: Facilities reports 3 tailgating incidents at your R&D building badge readers over 2 weeks — individuals following badged employees through without scanning. CCTV captured faces. The R&D building houses servers containing proprietary drug formulation research. What is your first action?

mitre.description: Physical tailgating bypasses logical access controls to gain proximity to sensitive systems — a classic precursor to hardware implant or direct workstation attacks.

choices.text: Escalate as a security incident. Share CCTV captures with Corporate Security and law enforcement. Audit badge logs for pattern analysis. Implement anti-tailgating controls (mantrap or officer briefing). Alert IT to monitor for unusual after-hours R&D workstation logins.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Physical incidents have direct cyber implications — tailgating often precedes USB drops, hardware implants, or direct workstation access. Correlating physical and cyber telemetry is mature convergence practice.

choices.text: Brief R&D staff on tailgating awareness and ask them to be more vigilant.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. A repeated pattern requires structural controls — mantrap or security officer — not just cultural reminders.

choices.text: Physical security is Facilities' responsibility — no action needed from IT Security.
choices.feedback: SILO FAILURE. Physical security incidents are a cyber concern. The convergence of physical and cyber domains is well-documented. Refusing to engage because 'it's Facilities' is precisely the gap threat actors exploit.

injects.title: Rogue Network Implant Discovered
injects.story: IT discovers a Raspberry Pi with a 4G cellular modem taped behind a network switch in the R&D server room. It has an Ethernet cable patched in and was installed approximately 10 days ago — consistent with the tailgating timeline. What do you do?

mitre.description: Attacker physically installed a rogue network implant providing persistent remote access via cellular out-of-band C2 channel, bypassing all perimeter network controls entirely.

choices.text: Do NOT power off the device yet. Photograph it in-place for evidence. Capture its MAC address and check DHCP/NAC logs. Contact your IR retainer and law enforcement. THEN isolate the switch port. Treat the entire R&D network segment as fully compromised for the past 10 days.
choices.feedback: FORENSICALLY CORRECT. Photographing in-place, capturing MAC/DHCP history, and reviewing outbound C2 traffic before isolation maximizes intelligence and preserves evidence. Treating the segment as compromised for 10 days is the correct blast radius assumption.

choices.text: Unplug the device, reboot the switch, and increase monitoring on the R&D network.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL. Isolation is correct but unplugging without documentation compromises forensic integrity. The 10-day compromise window requires investigation before declaring the network clean.

choices.text: Immediately unplug the device and dispose of it — it is clearly malicious.
choices.feedback: EVIDENCE DESTRUCTION. Disposing of a forensic artifact eliminates chain-of-custody for criminal prosecution. The device's SD card contains C2 communication history and attacker tooling critical to the investigation.

injects.title: Research Database Exfiltrated
injects.story: Cellular traffic logs (obtained via law enforcement carrier request) show the attacker accessed the proprietary drug formulation database and exfiltrated approximately 40 GB — 3 years of Phase II clinical trial data for your lead compound. A competitor filed a suspicious patent application yesterday.

mitre.description: Attacker exfiltrated proprietary pharmaceutical research via the rogue cellular implant, bypassing all network monitoring controls completely.

choices.text: Preserve all evidence for trade secret litigation. Notify FBI Cyber Division and FBI IP theft unit. File an emergency trade secret injunction against the competitor's patent application. Engage IP litigation counsel. Notify FDA if clinical trial data integrity was compromised.
choices.feedback: CORRECT MULTI-FRONT RESPONSE. Trade secret theft requires parallel legal and law enforcement tracks. Emergency patent injunctions can halt a competitor's application. FDA notification may be required for clinical trial data integrity. Timing is critical on all fronts.

choices.text: Send a cease-and-desist letter to the competitor about their patent application.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY APPROPRIATE BUT INSUFFICIENT. A C&D is a valid first step but trade secret theft of this magnitude requires FBI involvement and injunctive relief, not just a letter a competitor can ignore.

choices.text: Take no legal action against the patent — there is no legal proof the competitor used stolen data.
choices.feedback: MISSED LEGAL WINDOW. Emergency injunctions in patent proceedings have strict timing windows. Waiting forfeits the injunctive remedy. Circumstantial evidence — timing of application vs. breach — is sufficient to seek preliminary relief.

injects.title: No Network Access Control Exists
injects.story: Post-incident review reveals the R&D network has no NAC (Network Access Control) — any device plugged into a switch port gets a DHCP address and full network access. 23 unused active switch ports exist in publicly accessible areas of the building.

mitre.description: Lack of 802.1X NAC allowed an unauthorized rogue device to obtain network access simply by connecting to an active switch port — no authentication required.

choices.text: Implement 802.1X NAC requiring device certificate authentication before any switch port grants network access. Disable all 23 unused switch ports immediately. Deploy Network Behavior Analytics to detect rogue devices. Physically audit all network closets quarterly.
choices.feedback: CORRECT ARCHITECTURE. 802.1X NAC with certificate-based authentication means a rogue implant cannot obtain network access regardless of physical switch access. Disabling unused ports eliminates the attack surface immediately.

choices.text: Add more security cameras to the server room and adjacent hallways.
choices.feedback: DETECTIVE ONLY. Cameras detect but don't prevent. NAC is a preventive control that would have blocked this device regardless of physical access. Cameras alone don't solve the network access gap.

choices.text: Install a stronger lock on the server room door.
choices.feedback: WRONG PERIMETER. The rogue device was connected to a switch accessible in the R&D building — not necessarily the server room. Physical lock improvements without NAC leave every accessible switch port as an attack vector.

injects.title: Economic Espionage Act Decision
injects.story: FBI has identified a suspect linked to a competitor. The Economic Espionage Act (EEA, 18 U.S.C. §1831) applies — trade secret theft for the benefit of a foreign government carries up to 15 years imprisonment. Your Board wants to know: pursue criminal prosecution, civil litigation, or both?

mitre.description: Post-incident legal strategy for trade secret theft — criminal prosecution under EEA and civil litigation under DTSA are complementary and can be pursued simultaneously.

choices.text: Support BOTH criminal prosecution (cooperate fully with DOJ/FBI) AND file civil litigation under the Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA). The tracks are complementary — criminal prosecution deters future actors while civil litigation seeks damages and injunctive relief.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY OPTIMAL. EEA prosecution and DTSA civil litigation are designed to be pursued in parallel. FBI cooperation strengthens your civil case through shared evidence, and criminal conviction creates collateral estoppel advantages in civil proceedings.

choices.text: Pursue civil litigation only — criminal prosecution takes too long and the business needs certainty.
choices.feedback: SUBOPTIMAL. Civil litigation alone provides weak deterrence. EEA prosecution provides the strongest deterrence signal and may result in asset seizure. Timelines can proceed simultaneously — civil and criminal are not mutually exclusive.

choices.text: Settle quietly with the competitor for undisclosed compensation to avoid public disclosure.
choices.feedback: SHORT-TERM THINKING. A quiet settlement provides no deterrence, may trigger shareholder litigation for failing to protect IP adequately, and forfeits the intelligence value of public prosecution in deterring future espionage actors.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Silent Miner
scenario_meta.subtitle: Cloud Cryptojacking via Exposed Credentials
scenario_meta.estimated_impact: $180K Unauthorized Cloud Spend + Customer PII Breach

injects.title: Cloud Bill Anomaly Alert
injects.story: AWS sends a billing anomaly: your monthly spend jumped from $45K to $220K in 3 weeks. CloudWatch shows EC2 instance count grew from 40 to 340 — 300 unknown instances in us-east-2, a region your team never uses. No change tickets exist. What is your first action?

mitre.description: Attacker used compromised cloud credentials to launch hundreds of EC2 instances for cryptocurrency mining, generating massive unauthorized spend.

choices.text: Declare a cloud security incident. Use CloudTrail to identify which IAM credentials launched the rogue instances. Quarantine those credentials. Terminate all 300 unauthorized instances. Enable CloudTrail in ALL regions if not already active.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. CloudTrail identifies exactly which IAM principal launched the instances and from where. Terminating rogue instances stops the financial bleeding. Multi-region CloudTrail coverage is a common gap attackers exploit.

choices.text: Contact AWS support to dispute the charges and wait for their investigation.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL. AWS support is appropriate for billing recovery but cannot substitute for the security response. Every hour of delay costs ~$4,600 more in unauthorized compute. Terminate the instances first, then dispute charges.

choices.text: Terminate all 300 instances and assume it was a billing error.
choices.feedback: INCOMPLETE. Terminating instances is correct but the compromised IAM credentials remain active — the attacker can relaunch new instances within minutes. Root cause must be identified and remediated.

injects.title: Credential Exposed in Public Repo
injects.story: CloudTrail shows the rogue instances were launched using an AWS Access Key belonging to your CI/CD pipeline service account. GitHub's secret scanning (delayed 4 days) shows this key was accidentally committed to a public repository. The key has been publicly exposed for 4 days.

mitre.description: Developer accidentally committed AWS access keys to a public GitHub repo; automated scanning bots harvested the credentials within minutes of publication.

choices.text: Immediately revoke the compromised access key in the AWS console. Review ALL CloudTrail events for that key over 4 days for full blast radius. Rotate ALL CI/CD pipeline credentials as a precaution. Implement GitHub secret scanning and pre-commit hooks org-wide.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Credential revocation stops ongoing abuse. Full 4-day CloudTrail blast-radius review is essential — cryptomining may not be the only action taken. Pre-commit hooks prevent recurrence across all developers.

choices.text: Ask the developer to delete the commit from GitHub history and rotate their personal access token.
choices.feedback: TECHNICALLY MISGUIDED. GitHub history deletion doesn't remove secrets from forks, cached versions, or automated scrapers that harvested them within minutes. The AWS key must be revoked from the AWS console — git history edits are irrelevant now.

choices.text: Terminate all rogue instances and consider the incident resolved.
choices.feedback: INCOMPLETE. The compromised access key is still active — the attacker relaunches instances within minutes of termination. Revoking the credential is the required step, not just cleaning up its current effects.

injects.title: Customer PII Also Accessed
injects.story: Deeper CloudTrail analysis reveals the compromised CI/CD key had S3 read permissions. The attacker accessed 'prod-customer-exports' containing PII for 12,000 SaaS customers — 2 days into the 4-day exposure window. This occurred 2 days before you detected the incident. Is this a breach?

mitre.description: Attacker pivoted from cryptomining to opportunistic data collection, accessing customer PII stored in S3 using the over-privileged CI/CD credentials.

choices.text: Yes — treat S3 PII access as a confirmed breach. Engage Legal for GDPR/CCPA notification assessment. Notify cyber insurance. Begin breach notification preparation for 12,000 customers. Remove S3 read permissions from the CI/CD service account as least-privilege remediation.
choices.feedback: CORRECT CLASSIFICATION. Unauthorized access to PII-containing storage by attacker-controlled credentials constitutes a breach under GDPR, CCPA, and most state breach laws. The notification clock starts at discovery. Least-privilege remediation is mandatory.

choices.text: The attacker was primarily mining crypto — they probably didn't review the customer data. Wait for evidence of misuse before classifying as a breach.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY INCORRECT. Breach classification doesn't require evidence of data misuse — unauthorized access to PII by an unauthorized party IS the breach event. 'Probably didn't look at it' is not a legal standard under GDPR or CCPA.

choices.text: Revoke the key, restrict the bucket access, and document internally without external notification.
choices.feedback: NON-COMPLIANT. Making a bucket private after unauthorized access doesn't undo the access. Internal-only documentation when mandatory regulatory notification obligations exist violates both GDPR and state breach laws.

injects.title: Cloud Posture Gaps Identified
injects.story: Post-incident review: no SCPs at the AWS Organizations level, no GuardDuty enabled, no CloudTrail in 5 regions, 47 IAM users with AdministratorAccess, and service accounts with unnecessary console access. Your CTO wants a priority-ordered remediation plan.

mitre.description: Lack of multi-region CloudTrail meant attacker activity in unused regions was completely invisible — a common detection gap exploited by cloud attackers.

choices.text: Priority order: (1) Enable GuardDuty in all regions immediately. (2) Enable organization-wide multi-region CloudTrail. (3) Implement SCPs blocking instance launches in unused regions. (4) Apply least-privilege IAM and remove console access from service accounts. (5) Set Budget alerts at 120% of baseline.
choices.feedback: CORRECT PRIORITY ORDERING. GuardDuty first for immediate threat detection. CloudTrail second for forensic coverage. SCPs third to prevent recurrence. IAM fourth to reduce blast radius. Budget alerts as a financial detective layer. This follows the AWS Security Hub recommended sequence.

choices.text: Hire more cloud security engineers before making architectural changes.
choices.feedback: WRONG SEQUENCE. Hiring takes months; these are one-day configuration changes. GuardDuty and CloudTrail can be enabled in hours. Delaying basic security controls while awaiting headcount is not defensible risk management after a confirmed breach.

choices.text: Manually review CloudWatch logs daily to detect future incidents.
choices.feedback: DETECTIVE-ONLY AND UNSCALABLE. Manual log review misses the root causes: excessive IAM permissions (preventive), unused region access (preventive), and no automated detection (GuardDuty). Preventive architecture changes must come first.

injects.title: AWS Billing Dispute
injects.story: Your final bill includes $175K in unauthorized compute charges. AWS's abuse team confirmed the activity was unauthorized. You have CloudTrail forensic evidence of the credential compromise. AWS typically credits unauthorized charges when customers demonstrate a security incident. What is your approach?

mitre.description: Post-incident cloud billing recovery process — AWS has an established abuse credit process requiring forensic documentation of unauthorized access.

choices.text: File a formal AWS abuse claim with CloudTrail forensic evidence showing unauthorized access, timeline of credential compromise, and remediation steps taken. Escalate via your AWS Account Manager (Enterprise Support). Check cyber insurance for cloud abuse coverage in parallel.
choices.feedback: CORRECT PROCESS. AWS has an established abuse credit process — forensic evidence significantly strengthens your claim. Enterprise Support escalation bypasses standard queues. Cyber insurance cloud abuse riders are increasingly common and should be checked in parallel.

choices.text: Dispute all charges via the AWS billing console without supporting documentation.
choices.feedback: UNDEREQUIPPED. Billing disputes without forensic documentation of the credential compromise result in denial. AWS requires evidence that charges resulted from unauthorized access — not just disagreement with the bill.

choices.text: Pay the $175K and move on — it is faster than a dispute process.
choices.feedback: UNNECESSARY FINANCIAL LOSS. AWS routinely credits unauthorized charges with proper documentation — this is a recoverable loss. Paying without attempting recovery forfeits what is likely a full or partial credit and fails the organization's fiduciary duty.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Smishing Storm
scenario_meta.subtitle: SMS Phishing Targeting Executives via Unmanaged Devices

injects.title: Executive Smishing Campaign
injects.story: Three executives report receiving SMS messages impersonating your IT helpdesk: 'URGENT: Your VPN access expires today. Verify at: corp-vpn-verify[.]com.' One executive clicked the link. Two did not. MDM shows the clicking executive uses an unmanaged personal device for corporate email. What do you do?

mitre.description: SMS-based phishing targeting executives exploits unmanaged personal devices that lack MDM enrollment, mobile threat defense, and conditional access policies.

choices.text: Treat the clicking executive's credentials as compromised. Disable their accounts and require MDM re-enrollment before restoring access. Block corp-vpn-verify[.]com at DNS. Brief all executives on smishing. Implement Conditional Access requiring MDM-enrolled devices for corporate email.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Credential compromise assumption for any device visiting a credential-harvesting site is the right posture. The MDM enrollment gap is the root cause — Conditional Access requiring managed devices would have prevented this exposure.

choices.text: Send an IT helpdesk clarification email to all staff explaining the fake SMS.
choices.feedback: AWARENESS ONLY. Clarification is appropriate but doesn't address the likely compromised executive credential. The account must be treated as harvested until forensic analysis proves otherwise.

choices.text: The executive only clicked a link — no credentials were entered, so no action is needed.
choices.feedback: ASSUMPTION ERROR. Modern credential-harvesting sites can deliver drive-by exploits, install mobile malware, or load pre-filled credential prompts. Clicking a malicious link cannot be assumed safe without device forensic analysis.

injects.title: AiTM Session Hijack Confirmed
injects.story: M365 Defender alerts: the smishing target's account shows an active session from an Andorran IP while the executive is physically in Chicago. Sign-in logs confirm an AiTM phishing kit was used — the proxy captured both their credentials AND session cookie, bypassing TOTP MFA entirely. The attacker has an authenticated session right now.
