mitre.description: Attacker used an AiTM real-time proxy to capture both credentials and authenticated session cookies, bypassing standard TOTP-based MFA — a well-documented technique that only FIDO2 prevents.

choices.text: Revoke all active sessions for the executive's account immediately (M365 'Sign out everywhere' + token revocation). Temporarily disable the account. Review all M365 audit logs for emails read, forwarding rules created, and data accessed during the active session. Recommend upgrading to FIDO2 MFA.
choices.feedback: TECHNICALLY CORRECT. Session token revocation is required to evict an attacker using a stolen authenticated session cookie — a password reset alone does NOT invalidate it. FIDO2 phishing-resistant MFA is the only control that prevents AiTM entirely.

choices.text: Force a password reset on the executive's account.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. A password reset doesn't invalidate the stolen session cookie — the attacker's browser session remains valid regardless of a credential change. Session revocation at the application layer is the required action.

choices.text: Block the Andorran IP address and monitor for further suspicious logins.
choices.feedback: IP BLOCKING IS INEFFECTIVE. The attacker switches IPs immediately. The active authenticated session — not the IP — is the threat. The session must be revoked at the application layer, not blocked at the network layer.

injects.title: Brand Fraud Campaign Launched
injects.story: The compromised executive account was used to access your CRM API and send smishing messages to your entire customer database (800,000 customers) directing them to a fake 'free gift card' site harvesting payment card numbers. Customers are calling your contact center in high volumes.

mitre.description: Attacker weaponized compromised executive access to launch a large-scale customer fraud campaign using the brand's own CRM communication channels.

choices.text: Immediately revoke the CRM API token used. Send an emergency advisory via official channels warning customers the previous messages were fraudulent. Brief PR and prepare a public statement. Submit the fraudulent site to hosting providers for takedown. Notify the FTC and relevant state AGs.
choices.feedback: COMPREHENSIVE. Rapid customer warning via official channels limits fraud victims. Hosting provider takedown requests often succeed within hours. FTC and AG notification is required for consumer fraud at this scale.

choices.text: Take down your entire CRM system to prevent further API abuse.
choices.feedback: OVERCORRECTION. CRM takedown disrupts legitimate customer service operations. Revoking the specific API token achieves containment without the operational impact of a full CRM outage.

choices.text: Let customer service handle the inbound calls — avoid public statements that could amplify panic.
choices.feedback: HARMFUL INACTION. While you wait, customers actively submit payment card data to fraudsters — hundreds of victims per hour. Silence amplifies the crisis. A prompt official warning is always better than rumors filling the vacuum.

injects.title: PCI DSS Scope Assessment
injects.story: Legal raises a concern: 800,000 customers were directed to a fraudulent payment site via your brand's CRM. While your systems didn't store the card data, your brand and CRM were used as the delivery mechanism. Does PCI DSS apply? Your QSA is on the phone.

mitre.description: Post-incident PCI DSS scope analysis following brand-impersonation fraud — determining whether cardholder data environment compromise triggers forensic investigation obligations.

choices.text: Engage your QSA immediately for a formal scope opinion. Assess whether the CRM breach touches any cardholder data environment (CDE). Determine if payment brand notification is required. Engage a PCI Forensic Investigator (PFI) if the QSA advises it.
choices.feedback: CORRECT PROCESS. PCI DSS forensic requirements are complex — QSA engagement is the right first step. Even if your systems weren't the direct fraud source, payment brand notification may be required depending on CDE scope assessment.

choices.text: PCI DSS doesn't apply — you didn't store any card data from the fraudulent site.
choices.feedback: OVERSIMPLIFIED. PCI DSS scope analysis is complex and not limited to data storage. A QSA assessment is required — not a unilateral conclusion based on a simplified understanding of scope.

choices.text: Ignore the PCI question and focus entirely on customer communications.
choices.feedback: COMPLIANCE AVOIDANCE. PCI DSS non-compliance findings following a breach can result in $5K–$100K/month fines per payment brand and loss of card processing privileges — an existential risk for a retail organization. This cannot be deferred.

injects.title: Mobile Security Program Design
injects.story: Post-incident review: 40% of executives use unmanaged personal devices for corporate email; 78% use TOTP MFA (vulnerable to AiTM). These two gaps enabled the entire incident. What comprehensive mobile security program do you recommend to the Board?

mitre.description: Post-smishing mobile security architecture addressing MDM enrollment, phishing-resistant MFA, and executive device security requirements.

choices.text: Recommend: Mandatory MDM enrollment (Intune/Jamf) for all corporate email access, FIDO2 hardware keys or platform authenticators for all executive accounts, Conditional Access requiring compliant device + phishing-resistant MFA, and Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) on all managed devices.
choices.feedback: COMPLETE MOBILE ARCHITECTURE. MDM ensures device compliance. FIDO2 defeats AiTM (session cookies are cryptographically bound to the device). Conditional Access enforces both simultaneously. MTD provides runtime mobile threat detection. This architecture would have prevented this entire incident.

choices.text: Upgrade all executives from TOTP to push notification MFA apps.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT UPGRADE. Push notification MFA is still vulnerable to MFA fatigue attacks and AiTM proxy techniques. Only FIDO2/WebAuthn phishing-resistant authentication is fully resistant to AiTM — push notifications are not.

choices.text: Ban executives from using personal devices for any work purposes.
choices.feedback: IMPRACTICAL. Blanket bans create shadow IT — executives find workarounds that create less visible risk. MDM enrollment of personal devices (BYOD/MAM policy) with Conditional Access is workable, enforceable, and protects corporate data without blanket prohibition.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Broken Gate
scenario_meta.subtitle: SQL Injection & Web Application Data Breach

injects.title: Pentest Report Unresolved
injects.story: A penetration test from 6 months ago identified a Critical SQL injection vulnerability in your customer login portal (CVSS 9.8). The remediation ticket has been open for 180 days, stalled in the development backlog. A new OWASP advisory warns of active exploitation of similar vulnerabilities in retail portals. What is your escalation action?

mitre.description: Unpatched SQL injection in a public-facing web application is one of the most commonly exploited vulnerability classes, enabling direct database access.

choices.text: Escalate to executive leadership immediately — a 180-day unresolved Critical finding is a governance failure. Implement a WAF rule as an emergency compensating control today. Set a hard 2-week remediation deadline with daily standups.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. A 180-day open Critical pentest finding with active exploitation in the wild is an executive-level risk that cannot stay in a development backlog. WAF rules are a valid compensating control while code remediation is completed.

choices.text: Add the finding to the next quarterly risk committee agenda for prioritization.
choices.feedback: TOO SLOW. Active exploitation in the wild + 180-day open critical vulnerability = immediate escalation, not another quarterly review. If a breach occurs before the next committee meeting, this decision will be Exhibit A in any regulatory action.

choices.text: No action — the development team is already aware and has it in their backlog.
choices.feedback: NEGLIGENCE. Documented awareness of a critical vulnerability with no remediation timeline, followed by a breach, meets the legal definition of negligence in most jurisdictions. PCI DSS Requirement 6 mandates timely remediation of high-severity vulnerabilities.

injects.title: Database Dump on Dark Web
injects.story: A threat intelligence service alerts: a database dump containing 500,000 customer records (names, emails, hashed passwords, and 4-digit payment card CVVs stored in violation of PCI DSS) from your organization appeared on a dark web forum 12 hours ago. WAF logs confirm SQL injection attempts against the customer portal 3 days ago. What do you do?

mitre.description: Attacker exploited unpatched SQL injection to extract the entire customer database, including CVV data stored in violation of PCI DSS standards.

choices.text: Immediately apply WAF rules to block SQL injection patterns. Take the vulnerable portal offline pending emergency patching. Engage a PCI Forensic Investigator (PFI) — CVV storage is a critical PCI violation. Notify payment brands (Visa, Mastercard) per their breach notification requirements. Preserve all WAF and database logs.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. CVV storage violates PCI DSS Requirement 3 — this is a mandatory PFI engagement trigger. Payment brand notification has strict timelines (Visa: within 3 days of confirmation). Evidence preservation is critical for the PFI investigation.

choices.text: Apply a WAF patch and monitor for further attacks before notifying anyone.
choices.feedback: NON-COMPLIANT. CVV data storage violation + confirmed data on dark web = mandatory PFI engagement and payment brand notification. Monitoring without notification violates PCI DSS Requirement 12.10 and payment brand operating regulations.

choices.text: Delete the CVV data from the database immediately to remediate the PCI violation before anyone notices.
choices.feedback: EVIDENCE DESTRUCTION. Deleting data after a known breach is destruction of evidence, will be discovered by the PFI through transaction logs, and transforms a compliance violation into potential criminal obstruction charges. This is one of the worst possible responses.

injects.title: Fraudulent Card Transactions Reported
injects.story: Your card processor reports a spike in fraud disputes — 8,400 fraudulent transactions totaling $340,000 in the past 48 hours, all linked to cards from your customer database. Your issuing bank is demanding to know your incident response status. Card brands are threatening fines.

mitre.description: Stolen payment card data monetized through fraudulent transactions, triggering card brand fines and issuing bank disputes that create cascading financial and reputational impact.

choices.text: Provide your issuing bank and PFI with the full incident timeline. Cooperate fully with card brand investigations. Notify affected customers immediately with clear guidance on monitoring their statements and dispute procedures. File a SAR (Suspicious Activity Report) with FinCEN if required.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Full cooperation with card brands, timely customer notification, and FinCEN SAR filing (if applicable under your BSA obligations) demonstrates responsible incident management that can reduce card brand fines and civil litigation exposure.

choices.text: Dispute the card brand fines — the fraud originated from attacker actions, not yours.
choices.feedback: MISDIRECTED. Card brand fines are assessed for PCI DSS non-compliance (storing CVVs), not just for the breach itself. Disputing fines without addressing the underlying compliance violation is unlikely to succeed and delays remediation focus.

choices.text: Delay customer notification until the fraud scope is fully quantified to provide accurate information.
choices.feedback: COMPLIANCE FAILURE. Most state breach laws and PCI requirements mandate notification within specific timeframes — waiting for perfect information violates those timelines. Customers have a right to protect themselves from ongoing fraud immediately.

injects.title: Secure SDLC Gap Analysis
injects.story: The PFI confirms root cause: SQL injection in the login portal, CVV data stored in plaintext in violation of PCI DSS, no WAF deployed, and no Secure SDLC process requiring security testing before releases. Engineering wants to know what processes to implement to prevent a recurrence.

mitre.description: Absence of a Secure SDLC, pre-production security testing, and runtime application protection enabled a known critical vulnerability to reach production and remain unpatched for 6 months.

choices.text: Implement: parameterized queries / prepared statements as the code standard, SAST/DAST tools in the CI/CD pipeline, mandatory security code review for all authentication-related code, a WAF with OWASP Core Rule Set, and a formal vulnerability SLA (Critical: 15 days, High: 30 days).
choices.feedback: COMPLETE SECURE SDLC RESPONSE. Parameterized queries eliminate SQLi at the code level. SAST/DAST catches vulnerabilities pre-production. WAF provides runtime defense-in-depth. Formal SLAs with executive enforcement prevent future 180-day backlogs. This satisfies PCI DSS Requirement 6.

choices.text: Require all developers to complete an OWASP Top 10 training course.
choices.feedback: AWARENESS ONLY. Training is necessary but doesn't prevent vulnerabilities — developers make mistakes even with knowledge. Automated SAST tools in the pipeline catch vulnerabilities before they reach production regardless of developer awareness.

choices.text: Deploy a WAF and consider the remediation complete.
choices.feedback: INCOMPLETE. A WAF is a compensating control, not a code fix. The underlying SQLi vulnerability still exists in the codebase. PCI DSS Requirement 6 requires either application fixes OR a WAF with documented review — but the underlying vulnerability must still be tracked for remediation.

injects.title: PCI DSS Level Reassessment
injects.story: Your card processor has downgraded your PCI DSS compliance status and increased your transaction fees by 0.15% pending re-certification. The PFI has submitted their report to card brands. You estimate re-certification will take 6–9 months and cost $180K. The Board wants a clear roadmap.

mitre.description: Post-breach PCI DSS re-certification process requiring documented remediation of all findings, QSA re-assessment, and payment brand approval.

choices.text: Present the Board with a phased roadmap: (1) Emergency remediation of PFI findings within 30 days, (2) QSA gap assessment within 60 days, (3) Full Secure SDLC implementation within 90 days, (4) QSA re-assessment and SAQ/ROC submission within 6 months. Assign a dedicated PCI program manager.
choices.feedback: MATURE GOVERNANCE. A phased, time-boxed roadmap with executive ownership demonstrates to card brands and the Board that remediation is under active management. A dedicated PCI program manager ensures accountability through the 6-month re-certification process.

choices.text: Complete the PFI-required fixes and submit a new SAQ (Self-Assessment Questionnaire) to re-certify quickly.
choices.feedback: UNDERSCOPED. Following a Level 1 merchant breach, a self-assessment questionnaire is unlikely to be accepted by card brands — a full Report on Compliance (ROC) from a QSA is typically required. SAQ re-certification after a major breach may not be an available option.

choices.text: Switch payment processors to avoid the increased fees and compliance scrutiny.
choices.feedback: AVOIDANCE, NOT REMEDIATION. Switching processors doesn't reset PCI compliance status or eliminate card brand fines — those follow the merchant ID. New processors will require PCI compliance evidence before onboarding a recently-breached merchant.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Account Harvest
scenario_meta.subtitle: Large-Scale Account Takeover via Credential Stuffing

injects.title: Dark Web Credential Alert
injects.story: Your threat intelligence platform flags a dark web marketplace listing: 2.1M credentials for your bank's online portal are being sold for $800. Sample validation confirms 340,000 are currently valid. These likely originated from a third-party breach where your customers reused passwords. You have no MFA enforcement. What is your priority action?

mitre.description: Threat actor acquired a credential list from third-party breaches and is preparing a credential stuffing attack against your banking portal using validated active credentials.

choices.text: Trigger proactive forced password resets for all 340,000 validated accounts before attackers can act. Enable MFA enrollment prompts for all affected accounts. Implement rate limiting and bot detection on the login endpoint. Alert your fraud team to flag these accounts for heightened monitoring.
choices.feedback: PROACTIVE AND CORRECT. Forcing password resets before the attackers monetize the credential list is the most effective intervention. This is validated threat intelligence that enables a rare opportunity to act before the attack occurs.

choices.text: Monitor the dark web listing and wait to see if attacks actually materialize before acting.
choices.feedback: REACTIVE. You have validated intelligence that 340,000 active credentials are for sale. Waiting for attacks to materialize means waiting until after accounts are already compromised and funds potentially transferred.

choices.text: Issue a press release warning customers their credentials may be compromised.
choices.feedback: PREMATURE PUBLIC DISCLOSURE. A press release before implementing technical controls will cause panic and media scrutiny without protecting accounts. Forced password resets and MFA must come first — public communication comes after technical remediation is in place.

injects.title: Automated Attack Wave Detected
injects.story: Despite preparation, 180,000 login attempts hit your portal in 4 hours from 15,000 distinct IPs using residential proxies. 12,400 succeed — all against accounts that weren't in the forced-reset batch. SIEM shows classic low-and-slow credential stuffing pattern: 1 attempt per IP per 90 seconds, intentionally below your rate limit threshold.

mitre.description: Attacker used a residential proxy botnet with throttled request rates to evade rate limiting, successfully validating credentials across distributed source IPs.

choices.text: Deploy behavioral bot detection (device fingerprinting, mouse movement analysis, JavaScript challenges) rather than IP-based blocking. Reduce rate limit threshold to 1 attempt per 30 seconds. Force MFA step-up for all successful logins until the attack subsides. Alert fraud team on all 12,400 successful logins for manual review.
choices.feedback: TECHNICALLY CORRECT. Residential proxy networks defeat IP-based blocking — behavioral bot detection is required. MFA step-up for successful logins stops account takeover even with valid credentials. Fraud review of all successful logins is essential given the attack context.

choices.text: Block all 15,000 source IPs at the firewall.
choices.feedback: EASILY BYPASSED. Residential proxy networks rotate through millions of IPs. Blocklisting 15,000 IPs while the attacker rotates to 15,000 new ones provides minimal protection and creates management overhead.

choices.text: Take the login portal offline until the attack stops.
choices.feedback: SELF-INFLICTED OUTAGE. Taking a banking portal offline violates Regulation E availability obligations and your own SLA commitments. Behavioral detection and MFA step-up are surgical controls that stop ATO without denying service to legitimate customers.

injects.title: Fraudulent Transfers Initiated
injects.story: Of the 12,400 successfully accessed accounts, your fraud team identifies 847 accounts where fraudulent ACH transfers totaling $2.1M were initiated within 15 minutes of login. 223 transfers have already settled. What is your fraud containment sequence?

mitre.description: Attacker immediately monetized account access through fraudulent ACH transfers, exploiting the settlement window between initiation and clearing to maximize realized losses.

choices.text: Immediately recall all pending (not yet settled) ACH transfers via NACHA return codes. Lock all 847 affected accounts. File NACHA fraud returns for settled transactions. Notify FinCEN via SAR filing within 30 days. Contact receiving banks to attempt recovery of settled funds. Alert affected customers.
choices.feedback: CORRECT AND TIME-CRITICAL. ACH recall via NACHA return codes must happen within the settlement window — minutes matter. FinCEN SAR filing is mandatory for fraud exceeding $5,000. Receiving bank contact for fund recovery is a parallel track that occasionally succeeds even post-settlement.

choices.text: Lock all 847 accounts and wait for customers to contact you about the unauthorized transfers.
choices.feedback: PASSIVE. Locking accounts stops new transfers but waiting for customers to report fraud delays ACH recall attempts. Pending transfers must be recalled immediately — waiting means missing the recall window for unsettled funds.

choices.text: Continue monitoring — reverse the transfers only if customers formally dispute them per Regulation E.
choices.feedback: REGULATORY VIOLATION. Regulation E requires banks to investigate and resolve disputes within 10 business days and provisionally credit customers within 5 days. Waiting for formal disputes when you already know the transfers are fraudulent violates your Reg E obligations.

injects.title: MFA Architecture Decision
injects.story: Post-incident, executive leadership mandates MFA for all online banking customers. 2.1M customer accounts need an MFA solution. Options include: SMS OTP, TOTP authenticator apps, push notification, or FIDO2 passkeys. Budget is limited. What do you recommend and why?

mitre.description: MFA architecture choice determines resistance to SIM swapping, AiTM phishing, and SS7 interception attacks — not all MFA is equally secure.

choices.text: Recommend a phased approach: (1) TOTP authenticator apps as the default for all customers — free, phishing-resistant vs. SMS, and widely supported. (2) FIDO2 passkeys as the premium option for high-value accounts. (3) Explicitly deprecate SMS OTP within 18 months given SS7 and SIM swap vulnerabilities.
choices.feedback: STRATEGICALLY CORRECT. TOTP apps are dramatically more secure than SMS OTP (resistant to SS7 attacks and SIM swapping) and are free to deploy. FIDO2 passkeys for high-value accounts provides the highest security tier. Phased deprecation of SMS OTP is the right long-term posture for a financial institution.

choices.text: Deploy SMS OTP for all customers — it's the most familiar option and will have the highest adoption rate.
choices.feedback: ADEQUATE BUT SUBOPTIMAL. SMS OTP is better than no MFA, but it is vulnerable to SIM swapping and SS7 interception — well-documented attack vectors against banking customers. For a post-breach banking environment, TOTP is the minimum acceptable standard.

choices.text: Don't mandate MFA — it creates friction and customers will switch to competitors.
choices.feedback: REGULATORY NON-COMPLIANCE. FFIEC Authentication Guidance requires financial institutions to implement risk-based authentication. After a $2.1M fraud event enabled by absent MFA, choosing not to mandate it constitutes a documented regulatory compliance failure.

injects.title: FFIEC Examination Preparation
injects.story: Your primary federal regulator (OCC) has notified you of an upcoming IT examination with enhanced cybersecurity focus following the fraud event. The examination will assess authentication controls, fraud detection capabilities, third-party credential risk, and incident response. How do you prepare?

mitre.description: FFIEC examination preparation following a credential stuffing fraud event — demonstrating remediation, control improvements, and governance maturity to the primary federal banking regulator.

choices.text: Prepare a comprehensive remediation narrative: document what happened, root cause analysis, all control improvements made (MFA, bot detection, fraud monitoring), outstanding items with milestones, and Board-level oversight evidence. Engage external counsel experienced in OCC examinations for exam preparation.
choices.feedback: EXAMINATION-READY RESPONSE. Examiners assess governance maturity — a well-documented incident narrative with demonstrated remediation and Board oversight evidence typically results in a Matters Requiring Attention (MRA) rather than a more severe Matter Requiring Immediate Attention (MRIA) or enforcement action.

choices.text: Prepare only the documentation explicitly requested in the examination notice and nothing additional.
choices.feedback: MINIMALIST APPROACH. Providing only what is requested signals to examiners that the organization may not have a complete understanding of the incident or its remediation. Proactive documentation of improvements typically reduces examination findings.

choices.text: Engage legal counsel to limit examiner access and protect information under attorney-client privilege.
choices.feedback: ADVERSARIAL POSTURE. Attempting to limit OCC examiner access is both legally ineffective (examiners have statutory access rights) and strategically counterproductive. An adversarial examination posture is the fastest path to a formal enforcement action.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Broken Chain
scenario_meta.subtitle: Third-Party Vendor Breach Impacting Your Organization

injects.title: Vendor Notifies of Breach
injects.story: Your payroll processing vendor, PayrollPlus, notifies you that they suffered a ransomware attack 11 days ago. They are 'still assessing the scope.' Your employee PII (SSNs, bank account numbers, salary data for 3,200 employees) was in their system. They have not confirmed whether your data was exfiltrated. Your TPRM program has not audited PayrollPlus in 2 years. What is your first action?

mitre.technique: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Service Software
mitre.description: Threat actor compromised a payroll SaaS vendor, gaining access to the sensitive employee PII of all downstream customer organizations.

choices.text: Immediately engage PayrollPlus leadership for a formal briefing on the incident scope, demand their IR timeline and forensics status, request a list of your specific data elements confirmed or suspected to be in scope, and engage your Legal team to assess notification obligations based on what's known so far.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. You cannot manage what you cannot scope. Demanding formal briefings and specific data-element confirmation from the vendor is the first step. Legal engagement at this stage ensures notification timelines are tracked from the moment of vendor notification — not just from confirmation.

choices.text: Wait for PayrollPlus to complete their assessment before taking any action.
choices.feedback: COMPLIANCE RISK. State breach notification laws may start the clock from the date you received the vendor's notification — not from when the vendor confirms your data was affected. Passive waiting may already be putting you in violation of notification timelines.

choices.text: Do nothing — if your vendor is breached, it is their responsibility to handle it.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY INCORRECT. As the data controller (under GDPR) or covered entity holding responsibility for employee PII, you cannot delegate breach notification obligations to a vendor. The regulatory duty belongs to you, not PayrollPlus.

injects.title: Exfiltration Confirmed
injects.story: PayrollPlus confirms 5 days later: your employee data — SSNs, bank routing numbers, and salary data for all 3,200 employees — was exfiltrated before the ransomware deployed. The data appeared on the threat actor's dark web leak site yesterday. How do you proceed?

mitre.description: Attacker exfiltrated employee PII from the vendor environment before deploying ransomware — double extortion technique targeting the vendor's downstream customers.

choices.text: Classify as a confirmed breach. Notify all 3,200 affected employees with clear guidance (credit monitoring, fraud alerts). Notify your state AG per applicable breach law. Offer 2 years of credit monitoring at company expense. Alert your payroll bank to watch for ACH fraud using the exposed routing numbers.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. SSN + bank account number exposure is the highest-risk PII combination for identity theft and ACH fraud. Immediate employee notification, credit monitoring, and bank alerts address both the regulatory obligation and the duty of care to your workforce.

choices.text: Notify employees via a general email that 'some payroll vendor data may have been exposed' without specifics.
choices.feedback: INADEQUATE. Vague notifications without specific data elements and risk guidance fail both the spirit and letter of most state breach notification laws. Employees cannot protect themselves without knowing their SSN and bank data was confirmed exposed.

choices.text: Delay employee notification until you have fully reviewed all legal exposure — this is the vendor's fault.
choices.feedback: LIABILITY SHIFT IS NOT A DEFENSE. State breach notification laws do not provide exceptions because the breach occurred at a vendor. The notification obligation is yours as the employer holding employee PII — delay beyond statutory deadlines creates additional regulatory liability.

injects.title: ACH Payroll Fraud Attempted
injects.story: 72 hours after employee notification, your payroll bank flags 14 suspicious ACH debit attempts against employee bank accounts using routing and account numbers from the breach. Total attempted fraud: $218,000. One transfer of $14,500 already settled before the flag. What is your response?

mitre.description: Threat actor monetized exposed employee bank account details through direct ACH fraud, targeting individual employee accounts at their personal banking institutions.

choices.text: Immediately notify the payroll bank to place fraud holds on all 14 pending transactions. Contact the receiving bank for the settled $14,500 to initiate recall. Notify affected employees immediately with specific guidance on contacting their personal banks to place fraud alerts. File a SAR with FinCEN.
choices.feedback: TIME-CRITICAL AND CORRECT. ACH fraud holds on pending transactions must be placed within the settlement window. Receiving bank contact for fund recall occasionally succeeds even post-settlement. Employee-specific bank fraud alert guidance protects against future attempts.

choices.text: Notify the 14 affected employees and let them handle it with their personal banks.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL. Employee notification is correct but the employer's payroll bank must also be engaged immediately for holds on pending transactions — employees cannot recall ACH transactions through their personal banks without the originating bank's involvement.

choices.text: This is the employees' personal banking problem — not a corporate incident.
choices.feedback: DUTY OF CARE FAILURE. The fraud directly resulted from exposure of data your organization was responsible for. Employment law and common law duty of care obligations require active assistance to affected employees, not a hands-off posture.

injects.title: TPRM Program Gap Identified
injects.story: Post-incident review: PayrollPlus had no SOC 2 Type II report, no cyber insurance, no MFA on administrative consoles, and your TPRM program had not audited them in 2 years. Your organization processes payroll through 7 additional vendors with similar assessment gaps. What is your TPRM remediation plan?

mitre.description: Post-vendor-breach TPRM program remediation — addressing assessment frequency, contractual security requirements, and ongoing monitoring for all third-party vendors handling sensitive data.

choices.text: Tier all vendors by data sensitivity. Require annual SOC 2 Type II for Tier 1 vendors (those with access to sensitive PII). Add contractual MFA, encryption, and incident notification requirements to all vendor agreements. Implement continuous monitoring via a TPRM platform. Audit all 7 remaining payroll vendors within 30 days.
choices.feedback: MATURE TPRM GOVERNANCE. Risk-tiered assessment frequency, contractual security requirements, and continuous monitoring are the three pillars of an effective third-party risk management program per NIST SP 800-161r1 and most financial services regulatory guidance.

choices.text: Send an updated security questionnaire to all vendors and ask them to self-certify their controls.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. Vendor self-certification questionnaires without independent verification (SOC 2 reports, on-site assessments) have well-documented limitations. PayrollPlus would have passed a self-certification questionnaire — they had asserted adequate security to you previously.

choices.text: Replace PayrollPlus with a new vendor and consider the TPRM issue resolved.
choices.feedback: POINT SOLUTION. Replacing one vendor without fixing the TPRM program means the new vendor has the same unassessed risks as PayrollPlus did. The systemic gap — inadequate vendor oversight across all 7 remaining vendors — is unaddressed.

injects.title: Vendor Contract Liability
injects.story: Your Legal team has reviewed the contract with PayrollPlus. The indemnification clause is limited to $50,000 — far less than your total incident costs (employee notifications, credit monitoring, ACH fraud, legal fees) estimated at $420,000. PayrollPlus has no cyber insurance. Can you recover your losses?

mitre.description: Post-vendor-breach legal recovery analysis — contractual indemnification gaps highlight the importance of cyber insurance requirements in vendor agreements.

choices.text: Pursue the $50K indemnification per contract. File on your own cyber insurance policy for the remaining costs. Add mandatory cyber insurance minimums and unlimited breach indemnification clauses to all future vendor agreements. Use this incident to justify TPRM program budget to the Board.
choices.feedback: PRAGMATIC AND FORWARD-LOOKING. Recovering the contractual maximum and filing on your own policy addresses immediate costs. Future contract requirements for vendor cyber insurance and appropriate indemnification caps prevent this gap from recurring — and this incident is powerful Board-level justification for TPRM investment.

choices.text: Sue PayrollPlus for the full $420K despite the contract limitation.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY COMPLEX. Contractual indemnification caps are generally enforceable, and litigation against an already-breached vendor with no cyber insurance is costly and unlikely to yield recovery beyond the contractual limit. Legal fees may exceed any additional recovery.

choices.text: Accept the $50K and do not pursue further recovery — the legal costs would exceed the benefit.
choices.feedback: INCOMPLETE RESPONSE. While the PayrollPlus litigation analysis may be correct, this option ignores your own cyber insurance policy, which likely covers third-party vendor breach costs. Failing to file on available insurance coverage is a fiduciary failure.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Synthetic Voice
scenario_meta.subtitle: AI-Powered Deepfake Voice Social Engineering Attack

injects.title: Deepfake Threat Intelligence Briefing
injects.story: Your threat intelligence team flags an FBI advisory: AI-generated voice cloning is being used in BEC attacks. Threat actors clone executive voices using publicly available audio (earnings calls, YouTube interviews, podcasts) to instruct employees to wire funds. Your CFO gave a 45-minute podcast interview last month. Your finance team has no out-of-band verification protocol. What do you do?

mitre.description: Threat actors use AI voice synthesis models trained on publicly available executive audio to generate convincing voice deepfakes for real-time social engineering calls.

choices.text: Immediately establish a written out-of-band wire verification protocol requiring a callback to a pre-registered number for all transfers above $10K. Brief Finance and Executive teams on deepfake voice threats with audio examples. Establish a company-wide 'safe word' system for high-stakes voice authorizations.
choices.feedback: PROACTIVE AND CORRECT. Out-of-band verification breaks the deepfake attack chain entirely — even a perfect voice clone cannot authorize a transfer if the callback verification fails. Safe word systems add a second layer specific to deepfake defense.

choices.text: Send an awareness email about deepfake threats to all staff.
choices.feedback: AWARENESS WITHOUT CONTROLS. Email awareness alone is insufficient — employees under pressure from an authority figure (even a synthetic one) often comply. Procedural controls (callback verification, safe words) must accompany awareness training.

choices.text: No action needed — your employees would recognize a fake voice.
choices.feedback: DANGEROUS OVERCONFIDENCE. Modern AI voice cloning achieves indistinguishable quality from real audio. Multiple organizations have lost millions to deepfake voice calls where employees were certain they were speaking with their actual executive.

injects.title: Deepfake Voice Call Executed
injects.story: Your Finance Manager, Sandra, receives a call from what sounds exactly like your CFO: 'Sandra, I need you to wire $1.1M to a new vendor account immediately — we're closing a content licensing deal today. Don't discuss this with anyone yet, it's confidential.' Sandra wired the funds and only mentioned it to a colleague the next morning. How do you detect and respond?

mitre.description: AI-generated voice deepfake used to impersonate CFO in a real-time phone call, successfully authorizing a fraudulent wire transfer by exploiting authority and urgency cues.

choices.text: Immediately contact your bank to attempt a wire recall — timing is critical. Simultaneously call the real CFO via a known personal number to confirm they did not make this call. Preserve all call logs, metadata, and the receiving account details. File an FBI IC3 report and a SAR with FinCEN.
choices.feedback: TIME-CRITICAL AND CORRECT. Wire recalls must be initiated within hours — every minute matters. Confirming the CFO did not place the call establishes it as fraud. Call metadata and receiving account details are critical for FBI tracing. FinCEN SAR filing is mandatory.

choices.text: Interview Sandra thoroughly to verify her account before taking any action.
choices.feedback: WRONG PRIORITY. While Sandra's account is important, the wire recall window is measured in hours. Every minute spent on internal interviews instead of bank contact reduces recovery probability. Recall first, investigate simultaneously.

choices.text: Accept the loss — the wire has settled and there is nothing to do.
choices.feedback: INCORRECT. Wire recalls are possible even after settlement in some cases, particularly through correspondent bank chains. FBI involvement sometimes results in asset freezes at the receiving end. FinCEN SAR obligations also exist regardless of recovery prospects.

injects.title: Second Attack Attempt Identified
injects.story: 24 hours after the initial fraud, your SOC identifies a second deepfake voice attempt — this time targeting your Legal team, requesting that outside counsel wire a $450K retainer to a new firm account. The Legal Assistant hesitated and called Security. The call is ongoing. What do you do?

mitre.description: Attacker launched a second deepfake voice social engineering attempt within 24 hours, targeting a different department to maximize fraud before detection controls were implemented.

choices.text: Immediately instruct the Legal Assistant to politely end the call. Issue an emergency all-staff alert: all wire requests via phone must be verified via callback to a known number before processing — effective immediately, no exceptions. Preserve call metadata. Brief outside counsel directly via a known email.
choices.feedback: CORRECT REAL-TIME RESPONSE. Ending the active call stops the immediate threat. Emergency all-staff protocol implementation closes the attack vector enterprise-wide. Call metadata may help attribute the infrastructure used across both attacks.

choices.text: Ask the Legal Assistant to keep the caller on the line to gather more information.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL. Gathering information has intelligence value but risks the Legal Assistant making a mistake under continued pressure. The call should be ended by a Security team member or under explicit guided instruction.

choices.text: Allow the transfer to proceed to gather evidence of the attack methodology.
choices.feedback: UNACCEPTABLE. Allowing a known fraudulent transfer to proceed cannot be justified by intelligence-gathering rationale. This causes additional financial harm and creates serious fiduciary liability for decision-makers who authorized it.

injects.title: Audio Forensics & Attribution
injects.story: Digital forensics on the call audio confirms AI-generated synthesis. Metadata shows calls originated from VoIP numbers registered via cryptocurrency. FBI has the case but attribution is difficult. Your organization wants to know how to build technical detection capability for future deepfake calls.

mitre.description: AI voice synthesis combined with VoIP spoofing creates a dual-layer masquerade that defeats both caller ID verification and human voice recognition.

choices.text: Implement: real-time AI audio analysis tools that flag synthetic voice patterns for high-value calls, mandatory video verification for any authorization over $25K, caller ID verification policies (no action on spoofed numbers), and a vendor-agnostic authentication token shared only on verified channels.
choices.feedback: TECHNICALLY MATURE. AI audio analysis tools can detect synthetic voice artifacts in real time. Video verification defeats audio-only deepfakes. Caller ID policies eliminate spoofed number trust. Authentication tokens provide a zero-knowledge verification layer that deepfakes cannot bypass.

choices.text: Train employees to listen carefully for unnatural speech patterns in executive calls.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. Human audio detection of high-quality AI voice synthesis is unreliable — studies show humans cannot distinguish synthetic from real audio at rates better than chance. Technical controls are required, not trained human ears.

choices.text: Stop all phone-based authorizations permanently and require only email approvals.
choices.feedback: OVERCORRECTION. Emails are also spoofable and subject to BEC attacks. Eliminating phone-based authorization without implementing verified alternatives creates process gaps. A verified multi-channel approach is more robust than eliminating any single channel.

injects.title: Board Policy Update
injects.story: The Board has requested a formal policy update addressing AI-powered social engineering threats. No industry-standard framework currently has a specific AI deepfake control category. Your CISO must present a policy framework to the Board next week. What do you recommend?

mitre.description: Post-deepfake-fraud policy development addressing AI-powered social engineering — an emerging threat category not yet fully addressed by existing frameworks.

choices.text: Recommend a formal 'AI Social Engineering' policy addendum covering: mandatory video verification for high-value authorizations, pre-registered callback numbers for financial transactions, safe word protocols, employee simulation exercises, and quarterly review as the threat evolves. Map to NIST AI RMF 1.0 for governance credibility.
choices.feedback: GOVERNANCE-MATURE. Formalizing controls into policy with executive sign-off creates accountability. Mapping to NIST AI RMF 1.0 demonstrates awareness of the emerging AI governance landscape and provides an auditable framework reference for future regulatory inquiries.

choices.text: Update the existing BEC policy to add a line about deepfake awareness.
choices.feedback: UNDERSIZED RESPONSE. A one-line policy addition does not address the procedural, technical, and training changes required to defend against AI-powered social engineering. A dedicated policy section with specific controls is warranted given the demonstrated financial impact.

choices.text: Wait for regulatory guidance on AI threats before creating policy — premature policy may conflict with future standards.
choices.feedback: GOVERNANCE PARALYSIS. Waiting for regulatory guidance on an active, demonstrated threat is not an acceptable risk posture. Organizations are expected to respond to known risks with available controls regardless of whether specific regulatory guidance exists yet.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Flatline
scenario_meta.subtitle: Medical Device & Healthcare IoT Compromise

injects.title: Medical Device Inventory Gap
injects.story: A routine network scan discovers 340 unmanaged medical devices on your hospital network — infusion pumps, imaging systems, and patient monitors — none enrolled in your asset management system. Many run Windows XP Embedded or proprietary OS with no patch support. CISA has issued guidance warning hospitals that medical devices are being targeted. What is your first action?

mitre.description: Unmanaged, unpatched legacy medical devices on flat hospital networks represent high-value, low-security targets for ransomware actors seeking to disrupt patient care.

choices.text: Immediately build a complete medical device inventory with manufacturer, OS version, and patch status. Segment medical devices onto a dedicated VLAN isolated from general IT networks. Engage device manufacturers for available firmware updates. Brief clinical leadership on the risk landscape.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Network segmentation of medical devices onto isolated VLANs is the primary control for legacy devices that cannot be patched. Inventory is the prerequisite to any risk-based remediation. Clinical leadership briefing ensures operational continuity planning begins.

choices.text: Run a vulnerability scan against all medical devices to identify specific risks.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL AND RISKY. Active vulnerability scanning of medical devices can cause device crashes, interfere with clinical operations, and even patient safety events. Passive scanning and manufacturer consultation is safer. Network segmentation is more urgent than scanning.

choices.text: Medical devices are the clinical team's responsibility — escalate to the CMO and take no IT action.
choices.feedback: SILO FAILURE. Medical device cybersecurity is a joint responsibility of IT Security, Biomed Engineering, and Clinical leadership. HIPAA Security Rule and FDA cybersecurity guidance explicitly require hospital security teams to address connected medical device risks.

injects.title: Ransomware Hits Clinical Systems
injects.story: At 2:14 AM, ransomware begins encrypting files across your hospital network. By 2:31 AM: the EHR system is offline, imaging systems are down, and nursing stations cannot access patient records. The ED has 34 patients. ICU has 12 patients on monitored systems. Some infusion pump displays are showing error states. What is your immediate priority?

mitre.description: Ransomware deployed across hospital network impacts EHR, imaging, and potentially networked medical devices — creating simultaneous patient safety and cybersecurity emergency.

choices.text: PATIENT SAFETY FIRST: Immediately activate downtime procedures (paper-based clinical workflows). Physically verify all ICU patient monitors and infusion pumps for proper operation. Contact clinical engineering for emergency device assessment. Simultaneously begin IT network isolation. Notify hospital leadership and consider patient diversion for new ED admissions.
choices.feedback: CLINICALLY AND TECHNICALLY CORRECT. In healthcare, patient safety always takes priority over IT response. Downtime procedures maintain care continuity. Physical device verification (not network-based) is the safe approach during an active incident. Patient diversion protects incoming patients during reduced capacity.

choices.text: Focus on restoring the EHR system first — clinical staff cannot function without it.
choices.feedback: WRONG PRIORITY ORDERING. EHR restoration is important but the immediate threat is to patients already in the hospital. Downtime paper procedures must be activated first while IT restoration proceeds. Clinical care continuity comes before system restoration.

choices.text: Isolate the entire hospital network immediately to stop the ransomware spread.
choices.feedback: PATIENT SAFETY RISK. Blanket network isolation may disconnect networked life-critical devices from monitoring systems before clinical staff can manually assume oversight. Surgical network isolation with clinical safety checks must precede any broad containment action in a hospital environment.

injects.title: Patient Diversion & Downtime Operations
injects.story: Hospital is now on full downtime procedures. ED is diverting new patients. 47 current inpatients are being managed on paper-based workflows. Clinical engineering confirms ICU devices are operating on local/standalone mode — not network dependent. Ransomware has been isolated to the IT network. The ransom demand is 150 BTC ($9M). How long can you sustain downtime operations?

mitre.description: Extended clinical downtime in a hospital creates compounding patient safety risks as paper-based workflows degrade over time and staff fatigue sets in — a key pressure point ransomware actors exploit.

choices.text: Do not pay. Activate backup EHR (if available) or contract for emergency EHR access. Engage HHS, FBI, and CISA immediately — HHS has a Healthcare Cyber Task Force. Establish a clinical downtime sustainability assessment with CMO: what is the maximum safe downtime duration before patient transfer decisions must be made?
choices.feedback: CORRECT GOVERNANCE RESPONSE. HHS's Healthcare Cyber Task Force can provide rapid support including FBI coordination, CISA technical assistance, and guidance on peer hospital resource sharing. Downtime sustainability assessment is critical — clinical leadership must set the clock on when patient safety requires transfers.

choices.text: Pay the ransom — patient lives are at risk and 150 BTC is less than a prolonged downtime.
choices.feedback: HIGH RISK WITH POOR PRECEDENT. Payment may violate OFAC sanctions if the group is designated. Decryptors frequently fail or are slow in healthcare environments. FBI and HHS resources may make payment unnecessary. Paying funds criminal enterprise that specifically targets hospitals for this reason.

choices.text: Continue downtime operations indefinitely — paper workflows can sustain clinical care.
choices.feedback: UNSAFE ASSUMPTION. Prolonged hospital downtime creates measurable increases in adverse patient events, medication errors, and delayed diagnoses. Clinical leadership must set time-based decision points for patient transfer or external support — indefinite downtime is not clinically safe.

injects.title: EHR Restoration Sequence
injects.story: On day 3 of downtime, your backup systems are confirmed clean and restoration can begin. You have clean backups from 48 hours before the attack. The restoration sequence will take an estimated 18–24 hours. Clinical staff are fatigued. Which systems do you restore first and how do you validate clinical data integrity?

mitre.description: Healthcare system restoration requires clinical prioritization — not just technical recovery — ensuring patient safety and data integrity before systems are returned to clinical use.

choices.text: Restore in clinical priority order: (1) Pharmacy/medication systems, (2) Lab results, (3) Core EHR, (4) Imaging/PACS, (5) Administrative systems. Before going live, have clinical informatics and nursing leadership validate data integrity of active patient records against paper documentation from the downtime period.
choices.feedback: CLINICALLY CORRECT RESTORATION SEQUENCE. Pharmacy and lab systems have the most direct patient safety impact. Clinical data integrity validation against paper records is mandatory — discrepancies between electronic and paper records during the downtime gap could cause medication errors.

choices.text: Restore all systems simultaneously to get back to full operations as quickly as possible.
choices.feedback: OPERATIONALLY RISKY. Simultaneous restoration puts maximum load on recovery infrastructure and makes it harder to detect errors in any individual system. Phased restoration with validation checkpoints is safer and clinically more appropriate.

choices.text: Restore administrative and billing systems first — financial operations have been suspended for 3 days.
choices.feedback: WRONG PRIORITY. Billing systems have zero patient safety impact. Prioritizing administrative revenue recovery over clinical medication and lab systems during a healthcare emergency demonstrates governance values misalignment that will be reviewed by regulators and potentially plaintiffs.

injects.title: HHS OCR & State Health Department Review
injects.story: HHS Office for Civil Rights is reviewing whether the ransomware incident constitutes a HIPAA breach requiring notification of affected patients. The attack encrypted but did not necessarily exfiltrate PHI. Your Legal team argues no breach notification is required since no data was 'accessed.' HHS takes a different view. Who is correct?

mitre.description: HHS OCR's 2022 ransomware guidance states that ransomware incidents should be presumed to be HIPAA breaches unless the covered entity can demonstrate low probability of PHI compromise through a four-factor analysis.

choices.text: HHS is correct per their 2022 ransomware guidance. Ransomware incidents are presumed HIPAA breaches unless you can complete the four-factor low-probability-of-compromise analysis and document it. Conduct the analysis — if you cannot meet the standard, notify affected patients and HHS within 60 days.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY CORRECT. HHS OCR's 2022 guidance explicitly states ransomware infections are presumed to involve PHI access. The burden of proof for non-notification is on the covered entity via the four-factor analysis. Your Legal team's position, while intuitive, is inconsistent with HHS guidance.

choices.text: Your Legal team is correct — no notification required since no data was confirmed exfiltrated.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY INCORRECT. This is a common but dangerous misunderstanding. HHS OCR's ransomware guidance specifically addresses this argument and rejects it — encryption of PHI by an unauthorized party IS a disclosure under HIPAA, even without confirmed exfiltration. Relying on this position risks maximum regulatory penalties.

choices.text: Conduct the four-factor analysis but notify only if the analysis is inconclusive.
choices.feedback: PARTIALLY CORRECT. Conducting the four-factor analysis is the right first step. However, the standard is that notification is required unless you can affirmatively demonstrate low probability of compromise — inconclusive analysis means you must notify, not that you have discretion.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Root Access
scenario_meta.subtitle: Privileged Account Abuse & PAM Control Failure
scenario_meta.threat_actor: External Attacker via Compromised Admin Account

injects.title: Shared Admin Credential Alert
injects.story: An internal audit finds that your MSP's 40 technicians share a single domain admin credential 'msp_admin' across all 85 client environments — stored in a plaintext spreadsheet on a shared drive. A former technician left 3 months ago without credential rotation. Your PAM tool license expired 6 months ago. What is your immediate priority?

mitre.description: Shared privileged credentials stored in plaintext create a single point of catastrophic failure — compromise of one credential grants administrative access to all 85 client environments simultaneously.

choices.text: Emergency credential rotation: immediately rotate the shared admin credential across all 85 client environments. Simultaneously procure and deploy a PAM solution. Assign unique per-technician credentials with session recording. Notify clients of the credential hygiene gap per your MSA security obligations.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Shared credentials in plaintext with a departed employee's knowledge is an active compromise risk requiring immediate rotation — not a scheduled remediation. PAM deployment and client notification honor your MSP's contractual security obligations.

choices.text: Renew the PAM tool license and plan credential rotation for next month's maintenance window.
choices.feedback: TOO SLOW. A former employee with knowledge of a shared admin credential to 85 client environments is an active risk that cannot wait for a scheduled maintenance window. Emergency rotation is warranted.

choices.text: The former technician signed an NDA — there is no need to rotate credentials.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY AND TECHNICALLY NAIVE. NDAs do not prevent credential use — they create civil remedy after misuse. The credential must be rotated regardless of NDA status. If the former technician does misuse it, your failure to rotate despite knowing the risk creates negligence liability.

injects.title: Client Environments Compromised
injects.story: Before rotation completes, SIEM alerts fire across 12 client environments simultaneously: the shared 'msp_admin' credential is being used from a Bulgarian IP to deploy remote monitoring tools and exfiltrate data. The attacker is moving fast — a new scheduled task is being created in each environment every 4 minutes.

mitre.description: Attacker used compromised MSP admin credentials to move laterally across all 12 actively exploited client environments simultaneously, exploiting the shared credential's blanket administrative access.

choices.text: Emergency priority: rotate the compromised credential immediately across ALL 85 environments — not just the 12 actively attacked. Simultaneously notify all 85 clients of an active security incident. Engage your IR retainer for parallel response across affected environments. Contact FBI given the cross-client scope.
choices.feedback: CORRECT SCALE OF RESPONSE. If 12 environments are actively attacked, all 85 must be treated as compromised — the attacker has the credential for all of them. Simultaneous client notification is a contractual and ethical obligation. FBI engagement is appropriate given the multi-victim scope.

choices.text: Focus all resources on the 12 actively attacked environments and handle the other 73 later.
choices.feedback: SCOPE UNDERESTIMATION. The attacker has the credential to all 85 environments. While 12 are actively attacked now, the others are seconds away from attack if the attacker turns attention to them. All 85 must be treated as compromised simultaneously.

choices.text: Disconnect your RMM tool from all client environments to stop the attacker's access vector.
choices.feedback: ADDRESSES SYMPTOM NOT CAUSE. Disconnecting the RMM tool stops one access path but the attacker already has domain admin credentials — they can use any number of other remote access methods. Credential rotation is the only effective containment action.

injects.title: Client Data Exfiltrated
injects.story: Forensics confirms data exfiltration from 7 of the 12 actively attacked client environments. Client data includes: healthcare PHI (2 clients), financial records (3 clients), and employee PII (2 clients). Each client has their own regulatory notification obligations. As the MSP, what is your responsibility?

mitre.description: Attacker exfiltrated sensitive client data across multiple regulatory jurisdictions simultaneously, creating a cascade of parallel breach notification obligations across different frameworks.

choices.text: Immediately notify all 7 affected clients with full forensic detail of what was accessed and exfiltrated from their environments. Provide each client with a timeline and evidence package to support their own regulatory notifications. Your MSA likely makes clients the data controllers — they hold the notification obligation, but you must support them with evidence.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY CORRECT FOR MSP MODEL. In most MSP arrangements, clients are the data controllers and hold regulatory notification obligations. Your duty is to notify clients immediately and provide complete forensic evidence so they can meet their own timelines — HIPAA's 60 days, GDPR's 72 hours, state breach laws.

choices.text: Handle all client breach notifications centrally to provide a consistent message.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY PROBLEMATIC. Centralized breach notification by the MSP on behalf of clients may conflict with each client's own regulatory obligations, legal counsel direction, and specific notification content requirements. Clients must control their own notifications — your role is evidence and support.

choices.text: The breach was caused by an external attacker — you are not responsible for client breach notifications.
choices.feedback: CONTRACTUALLY WRONG. Your MSA almost certainly includes security incident notification obligations to clients. Regardless of attacker responsibility, your shared credential was the attack vector — clients will hold you contractually liable and your failure to notify promptly is an independent breach of contract.

injects.title: PAM Architecture Deployment
injects.story: Post-incident, you must rebuild your privileged access architecture across 85 client environments. The Board has approved budget for a full PAM deployment. Key requirements: unique credentials per technician per client, session recording for all privileged sessions, just-in-time access, and MFA for all admin access. How do you sequence the deployment?

mitre.description: Post-breach PAM architecture deployment for an MSP — implementing zero-standing-privilege and session recording across all client environments to eliminate shared credential risk.

choices.text: Deploy in risk-tiered order: (1) Healthcare and financial clients first (highest regulatory exposure), (2) All remaining clients within 90 days. Implement zero-standing-privilege — no persistent admin accounts, JIT access only. Deploy session recording for all privileged sessions. Enforce FIDO2 MFA for all technician logins to PAM.
choices.feedback: MATURE PAM ARCHITECTURE. Risk-tiered deployment addresses highest-exposure clients first. Zero-standing-privilege eliminates persistent credentials entirely — attackers cannot steal what doesn't exist at rest. Session recording satisfies both security and contractual audit requirements.

choices.text: Deploy PAM to your internal MSP environment first, then roll out to clients over the next year.
choices.feedback: WRONG PRIORITY ORDERING. The attack vector was the shared credential used IN client environments — not your internal MSP environment. Client environment PAM deployment is the urgent priority, not internal systems.

choices.text: Issue each technician a unique password for the shared admin account instead of full PAM deployment.
choices.feedback: PSEUDOSOLUTION. Unique passwords for the same shared account still means a single credential grants access to all 85 environments. PAM's value is in unique vaulted credentials per-client, session isolation, and JIT access — not just password uniqueness.

injects.title: Client Contractual Liability
injects.story: Four of your affected clients are threatening breach of contract litigation for failure to maintain adequate security controls as specified in their MSAs. Two are healthcare organizations with HIPAA Business Associate Agreements (BAAs). Legal estimates exposure of $2.1M in client claims. Your cyber insurance has a $1M sublimit for MSP liability. How do you respond?

mitre.description: Post-breach MSP contractual and BAA liability assessment — managing parallel legal exposure to client breach of contract claims and HIPAA Business Associate regulatory obligations.

choices.text: Engage specialized cyber breach litigation counsel immediately. Proactively offer mediation to the four clients — litigation is costly for both sides and demonstrates good faith. Notify your cyber insurer and engage coverage counsel. Review BAA obligations with the two HIPAA clients separately — BAA violations carry independent HHS exposure.
choices.feedback: STRATEGICALLY CORRECT. Proactive mediation often resolves breach of contract claims faster and at lower cost than litigation, while preserving client relationships. BAA obligations require separate HIPAA analysis — BAA breaches trigger independent regulatory exposure beyond the civil claims.

choices.text: Let your insurance carrier handle all client claims under the MSP liability sublimit.
choices.feedback: PARTIALLY CORRECT but the $1M sublimit is likely insufficient for $2.1M in exposure. Insurance handles covered claims but your legal team must simultaneously manage the coverage gap, the BAA regulatory exposure (which insurance may not cover), and client relationship preservation.

choices.text: Argue that the external attacker — not your MSP — is solely responsible for client damages.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY WEAK POSITION. Courts consistently hold service providers liable for security failures that contractually guaranteed controls would have prevented. The shared plaintext credential was your negligence — the external attacker exploited it. Both can be simultaneously liable.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Cold Restart
scenario_meta.subtitle: Data Center Outage & Disaster Recovery Failure

injects.title: DR Test Failure Discovered
injects.story: Your annual DR test reveals that your primary database cluster cannot failover to the DR site within the 4-hour RTO committed in your Business Continuity Plan. Actual failover time measured: 11.5 hours. The BCP has not been updated in 3 years. Core banking is in scope. Regulators expect RTO compliance. What is your immediate action?

mitre.description: A DR test failure reveals that documented recovery objectives are unachievable — a critical gap that becomes a regulatory and financial liability when an actual outage occurs.

choices.text: Escalate the RTO gap to executive leadership and the Board Risk Committee immediately. Update the BCP to reflect actual achievable RTO (11.5 hours) pending technical remediation. Notify your primary banking regulator of the gap proactively — regulators view self-disclosure far more favorably than discovering gaps during examinations.
choices.feedback: CORRECT GOVERNANCE RESPONSE. Continuing to represent an unachievable 4-hour RTO in your BCP is a material misrepresentation to regulators. Proactive disclosure with a remediation plan consistently results in better regulatory outcomes than discovered gaps.

choices.text: Schedule a re-test in 6 months after engineering works on the failover process.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. A 6-month timeline with an unachievable RTO on record creates regulatory exposure for every day in between. The BCP must be updated to reflect reality immediately, and a remediation timeline must be documented and disclosed.

choices.text: Keep the 4-hour RTO in the BCP — the test conditions were not representative of a real outage.
choices.feedback: MATERIAL MISREPRESENTATION. Knowingly maintaining an inaccurate RTO in a BCP submitted to regulators constitutes a material misrepresentation. When a real outage occurs and recovery takes 11.5 hours, regulators will compare against the documented 4-hour commitment.

injects.title: Primary Data Center Fire
injects.story: At 3:22 AM, a cooling system failure causes a fire suppression system activation in your primary data center. All servers are powered down by the suppression system. Core banking, online banking, ATM network, and card processing are all offline. 2.1 million customers cannot access accounts. Your DR site activation procedure is in a binder — in the primary data center that is now inaccessible. What do you do?

mitre.description: Physical data center outage requiring DR failover — the procedural gap of inaccessible DR runbooks compounds a hardware failure into a governance and recovery failure.

choices.text: Activate BCP command structure immediately. Use your team's knowledge and any off-site copies of runbooks (cloud storage, email archives) to begin DR site activation. Notify your banking regulator per required outage notification timelines (typically within 2–4 hours for core banking). Issue a public customer advisory via social media and website (DR site).
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Regulators must be notified of significant outages within defined windows — FFIEC guidance requires prompt notification for outages affecting a significant percentage of customers. Customer communication via alternative channels manages reputational damage. Runbook retrieval from off-site copies is standard DR preparation.

choices.text: Wait for the fire department to clear the building so you can retrieve the DR runbooks before starting recovery.
choices.feedback: TOO SLOW. Fire clearance could take hours. Every minute of additional downtime increases regulatory exposure and customer harm. DR recovery must begin with available resources immediately — runbook retrieval from memory, cloud copies, or team knowledge.

choices.text: Contact your data center vendor and wait for them to restore power before taking action.
choices.feedback: WRONG RESPONSE MODEL. Vendor power restoration may take many hours and does not activate your DR site. DR activation is your team's responsibility — waiting for the primary site to be restored when a DR site exists is a governance failure.

injects.title: ATM Network Offline — Cash Demand Spike
injects.story: Hour 6 of the outage. ATM network remains offline. Social media is reporting long lines at branches as customers demand cash. News outlets pick up the story. Your stock price is dropping in pre-market trading. Card processing came back online at hour 4 via the DR site, but core banking (account balances, transfers) remains offline. RTO is being missed.

mitre.description: Extended core banking outage creates cascading customer, reputational, and market impacts — the compounding effect of a single infrastructure failure when DR capabilities are inadequate.

choices.text: Prioritize ATM network restoration from the DR site — cash access is the most visible customer need. Coordinate with correspondent banks for emergency cash distribution at branches. Issue a detailed public update with estimated restoration timeline. Prepare a Board and regulatory briefing on the missed RTO with a remediation timeline.
choices.feedback: CORRECT STAKEHOLDER MANAGEMENT. ATM access is the most visible and urgent customer need. Correspondent bank coordination for emergency cash distribution demonstrates customer care. Transparent timeline communication manages reputational damage better than silence.

choices.text: Issue a social media post blaming the fire suppression system vendor and promising restoration 'soon.'
choices.feedback: POOR CRISIS COMMUNICATION. Blame-shifting to a vendor before investigation is complete creates legal liability and appears defensive. Customers want timeline and access, not vendor blame. 'Soon' is not an acceptable estimate for a regulated financial institution outage.

choices.text: Decline to comment publicly until full service restoration to avoid amplifying concerns.
choices.feedback: COMMUNICATIONS FAILURE. Silence during a major customer-impacting outage creates more anxiety and reputational damage than transparent communication. Regulators also expect proactive customer communication during significant outages.

injects.title: Primary Site Restoration
injects.story: Total outage lasted 14 hours — 10 hours beyond your documented 4-hour RTO. Primary site is now restored and DR failback is complete. No data loss confirmed. Your engineering team wants to know what infrastructure changes to make before the next potential event. What do you prioritize?

mitre.description: Post-outage infrastructure remediation to achieve documented recovery objectives — addressing the DR failover gap, runbook accessibility, and automated failover capabilities.

choices.text: Prioritize: (1) Automated DR failover for core banking — eliminate manual steps that caused the 11.5-hour actual RTO. (2) Store all DR runbooks in cloud-accessible, geographically separate locations. (3) Implement quarterly DR tests with documented results. (4) Establish a realistic RTO that engineering can commit to and test consistently.
choices.feedback: INFRASTRUCTURE-MATURE REMEDIATION. Automated failover eliminates the human coordination bottleneck that caused the 11.5-hour recovery. Cloud-stored runbooks prevent the 'binder in the burning building' anti-pattern. Quarterly testing with documented results satisfies regulatory examination requirements.

choices.text: Install additional fire suppression sensors to prevent future data center fires.
choices.feedback: ADDRESSES ONLY ONE FAILURE MODE. Additional fire detection is appropriate but doesn't fix the core DR gap — the 11.5-hour failover time. Any number of events (power, connectivity, natural disaster) could cause a primary site failure. The DR architecture itself must be fixed.

choices.text: Move entirely to cloud infrastructure to eliminate data center dependency.
choices.feedback: AVOIDANCE WITHOUT REMEDIATION. Proposing a multi-year serverless migration as the primary response to an active DR gap leaves the documented RTO failure unaddressed for years. Regulators and auditors expect a concrete near-term remediation plan — not a roadmap to a different architecture. The immediate automated failover fix cannot be deferred.

injects.title: Regulatory Examination Response
injects.story: Your primary federal banking regulator (OCC) has formally requested a post-outage briefing. They will review: your BCP documentation, the actual vs. committed RTO, your customer notification timeline, and your remediation plan. You previously self-disclosed the RTO gap. How does your self-disclosure affect the examination outcome?

mitre.description: Banking regulator examination following a significant outage — proactive self-disclosure of known gaps consistently results in better examination outcomes than discovered deficiencies.

choices.text: Present the examination with complete transparency: the DR test failure, the self-disclosure decision, the actual outage timeline, customer notification actions taken, and a specific remediation roadmap with committed dates. Self-disclosure demonstrates the governance maturity regulators value most.
choices.feedback: EXAMINATION-OPTIMAL POSTURE. Regulators universally treat self-disclosed gaps with more leniency than discovered gaps. Your proactive notification, transparent outage management, and specific remediation commitments position this as a Matters Requiring Attention (MRA) rather than a formal enforcement action.

choices.text: Present only the post-outage remediation plan and minimize discussion of the pre-existing RTO gap.
choices.feedback: COUNTERPRODUCTIVE. You already self-disclosed the RTO gap — attempting to minimize it now will appear inconsistent with your prior disclosure and may be interpreted as lack of candor with the regulator.

choices.text: Argue that the 14-hour outage was caused by the fire, not a DR failure, and that your BCP performed as designed.
choices.feedback: REGULATORY MISREPRESENTATION. You self-disclosed that the DR test showed an 11.5-hour actual RTO vs. a 4-hour committed RTO. The 14-hour outage is directly consistent with the known gap. Arguing otherwise contradicts your own prior self-disclosure and will severely damage regulator trust.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Broken Pod
scenario_meta.subtitle: Kubernetes Container Escape & Cluster Compromise

injects.title: Container Security Audit Gap
injects.story: A security audit flags your Kubernetes cluster runs containers as root, has no Pod Security Policies enforced, grants default service accounts overly permissive RBAC roles, and the Kubernetes API server is internet-accessible with only password authentication (no RBAC for external access). Engineering says 'containers are isolated by design.' What is your response?

mitre.description: Misconfigured Kubernetes clusters with containers running as root and excessive RBAC permissions enable container escapes that grant full cluster-admin access to attackers.

choices.text: Escalate immediately. Implement Pod Security Standards (restricted profile) to enforce non-root containers. Restrict Kubernetes API server access to corporate VPN only. Audit and reduce all service account RBAC permissions to least privilege. Enable Kubernetes audit logging.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Each finding represents a critical container security control gap. 'Containers are isolated by design' is false when running as root — a container escape vulnerability allows privilege escalation to the node host and potentially full cluster compromise.

choices.text: Accept the findings and schedule remediation for the next quarterly infrastructure sprint.
choices.feedback: TOO SLOW. An internet-accessible Kubernetes API server with weak authentication is actively scannable by attackers. Kubernetes is a primary target for cryptomining and data theft campaigns. Quarterly timeline is not acceptable for critical findings.

choices.text: Agree with Engineering — containers provide sufficient isolation and no changes are needed.
choices.feedback: TECHNICALLY INCORRECT. Container isolation is not equivalent to VM isolation. Running as root, missing Pod Security Standards, and excessive RBAC are well-documented paths to cluster compromise. Multiple real-world breaches have followed exactly this configuration.

injects.title: Cryptominer Deployed in Cluster
injects.story: Kubernetes audit logs (which you enabled last week) show a new namespace 'kube-system-update' was created via the API server from an external IP. Twenty pods are running an unrecognized image pulling from a public registry. CPU utilization across the cluster spikes to 94%. EDR on nodes shows xmrig (a cryptominer) running inside pods. What is the attack path?

mitre.description: Attacker gained access to the Kubernetes API server and deployed malicious workloads in a disguised namespace, using cluster compute resources for cryptomining as an initial low-risk foothold.

choices.text: Identify the API server auth method used for the unauthorized access (leaked credential, anonymous access, or compromised service account). Immediately delete the malicious namespace and pods. Rotate all Kubernetes service account tokens. Restrict API server access to VPN. Treat the cluster as potentially fully compromised — audit all namespaces for additional malicious workloads.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Cryptomining is often a low-risk probe before higher-impact activity. Identifying the authentication method used is critical — if anonymous access was enabled, the attack path is trivial and the scope is much wider. Full cluster audit is mandatory.

choices.text: Delete the malicious pods and patch the specific vulnerability the attacker used.
