choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT SCOPE. Deleting pods without identifying the authentication path leaves the attack vector open. The attacker can redeploy within minutes. Without full cluster audit, other malicious workloads may be missed.

choices.text: Restart the Kubernetes cluster to clear all running pods and start fresh.
choices.feedback: DESTROYS FORENSIC EVIDENCE. Cluster restart eliminates pod logs, network flow records, and runtime evidence needed to understand the full scope of compromise. Forensic preservation must precede remediation.

injects.title: Container Escape to Host Node
injects.story: Further forensics reveals the attacker escalated beyond cryptomining: they mounted the host filesystem from within a privileged container and accessed the node's Kubernetes service account token — granting cluster-admin privileges. With cluster-admin access, they read secrets from all namespaces, including database credentials for your production PostgreSQL cluster containing customer data.

mitre.description: Attacker exploited privileged container configuration to escape container isolation, access host node credentials, and escalate to cluster-admin — enabling access to all cluster secrets and workloads.

choices.text: Rotate ALL Kubernetes secrets and database credentials immediately — they are fully compromised. Isolate the affected nodes. Assess whether database access logs show unauthorized queries to customer data during the compromise window. If customer data was accessed, engage Legal for breach notification assessment.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Cluster-admin access to Kubernetes secrets means every database credential, API key, and certificate in the cluster is compromised. Full secret rotation is mandatory. Database access log analysis determines whether customer data breach notification obligations are triggered.

choices.text: Rotate only the database credentials that were directly accessed in the secrets audit.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. With cluster-admin access, the attacker could have read any and all secrets — not just the ones you can confirm they accessed. Selective rotation based on confirmed access understates the blast radius. All cluster secrets must be rotated.

choices.text: The container escape only affected the one node — other nodes are safe.
choices.feedback: INCORRECT. Cluster-admin privileges obtained via the node service account token apply to the entire cluster — not just the compromised node. The attacker can schedule pods on any node and access secrets in any namespace.

injects.title: Cluster Hardening Roadmap
injects.story: Post-incident, your engineering team must harden the Kubernetes cluster. The CTO wants a prioritized hardening checklist addressing the attack vectors exploited in this incident.

mitre.description: Post-breach Kubernetes cluster hardening addressing container escape paths, API server exposure, and secrets management gaps.

choices.text: Prioritized hardening: (1) Enforce Pod Security Standards — restricted profile, no privileged containers, no host path mounts. (2) Move secrets to HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager — not Kubernetes secrets. (3) Restrict API server to private network. (4) Implement network policies between namespaces. (5) Enable Falco for runtime threat detection.
choices.feedback: COMPREHENSIVE K8S HARDENING. Pod Security Standards eliminate the privileged container escape path. External secrets management (Vault/ASM) means even cluster-admin cannot read secrets in plaintext. Network policies limit blast radius. Falco provides runtime detection of escape attempts.

choices.text: Upgrade to the latest Kubernetes version and consider the hardening complete.
choices.feedback: NECESSARY BUT INSUFFICIENT. Kubernetes version upgrades are important but the attack in this scenario exploited misconfiguration, not a version-specific vulnerability. Configuration hardening is the primary remediation required.

choices.text: Migrate all workloads to serverless functions to eliminate container security concerns.
choices.feedback: DEFERRED REMEDIATION IS NOT REMEDIATION. A multi-year serverless migration plan does not address the immediate Kubernetes security gaps that enabled this breach. Regulators, auditors, and customers expect specific near-term technical controls — not a long-term platform migration as a substitute for fixing known misconfigurations today. The cluster must be hardened now, in parallel with any future architectural decisions.

injects.title: SOC 2 Type II Audit Impact
injects.story: Your organization holds a SOC 2 Type II certification used by enterprise customers in sales processes. Your auditor has been informed of the breach. The audit period overlaps with the compromise window. Control CC6.1 (Logical and Physical Access Controls) and CC7.2 (System Monitoring) are in scope. What is your response to your auditor?

mitre.description: Post-breach SOC 2 audit management — a breach during an audit period requires transparent disclosure to auditors and may result in a qualified opinion affecting customer trust.

choices.text: Provide full transparency to your auditor: disclose the incident, the affected controls, the duration of the control failure, and the remediation actions taken. A qualified opinion with disclosed exceptions and demonstrated remediation is far better than a withdrawn certification or a subsequent audit finding that the breach was concealed.
choices.feedback: AUDIT-INTEGRITY CORRECT. SOC 2 auditors have professional obligations — concealing a material breach from them during an audit period constitutes fraud. A qualified opinion with disclosed exceptions and remediation evidence is a recoverable audit outcome. Concealment is not.

choices.text: Ask the auditor to exclude the compromise window from the audit period scope.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL. Scope adjustments are sometimes permissible for legitimate reasons, but auditors will document the exclusion and its rationale. Customers reviewing the SOC 2 report will see the scope limitation and ask questions. Full transparency with documented remediation is typically a better customer-facing outcome.

choices.text: Do not disclose the breach to the auditor — the incident is being handled internally.
choices.feedback: AUDIT FRAUD. Concealing a material security incident from a SOC 2 auditor during an active audit engagement is fraud. When discovered — and auditors are specifically trained to find undisclosed incidents — it results in withdrawn certification, legal liability, and destroyed customer trust.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Consent Trap
scenario_meta.subtitle: Malicious OAuth App Consent Grant Attack

injects.title: Uncontrolled OAuth App Registrations
injects.story: An audit reveals employees have granted OAuth consent to 847 third-party applications in your Microsoft 365 tenant — most without IT approval. Among them: apps requesting Mail.Read, Files.ReadWrite.All, and Contacts.Read permissions. No admin consent policy exists. No monitoring of OAuth grant activity is in place. What is your first action?

mitre.description: Malicious OAuth apps with broad permission grants provide persistent, credential-independent access to user data — surviving password resets and MFA changes.

choices.text: Immediately restrict user OAuth consent to verified publisher apps only (Microsoft Entra admin consent policy). Audit all 847 existing grants and revoke any with excessive permissions or unknown publishers. Enable Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps to monitor OAuth activity going forward.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Admin consent policies prevent future malicious app grants. Auditing existing grants identifies currently active malicious access. OAuth token access survives password changes — revocation must be explicit. Defender for Cloud Apps provides ongoing detection.

choices.text: Send a communication asking employees to review their own app consents and remove any they don't recognize.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. User self-review of 847 apps is unreliable and slow. Employees cannot effectively distinguish legitimate from malicious OAuth apps. Admin-level revocation of suspicious grants is required, not voluntary user cleanup.

choices.text: OAuth apps are a user convenience feature — no action needed unless a specific app causes problems.
choices.feedback: DANGEROUS POSTURE. Uncontrolled OAuth consent is a well-documented attack vector (IllusionBlack, Consent Phishing campaigns). Apps with Mail.Read access to executive mailboxes provide persistent BEC-enabling intelligence access that survives all credential rotation.

injects.title: Malicious App Identified
injects.story: Your OAuth audit identifies an app called 'Microsoft Teams Enhancer Pro' — not a Microsoft product — that 12 employees granted Mail.ReadWrite, Contacts.Read, and Files.ReadWrite.All permissions to 3 weeks ago. The app's publisher domain (microsoft-teams-pro[.]com) was registered 4 weeks ago. Audit logs show the app accessed 3 executive mailboxes daily since grant.

mitre.description: Malicious OAuth app with Mail.ReadWrite permissions provides persistent, credential-independent email access — reading, exfiltrating, and potentially manipulating executive email without triggering MFA or password-based detection.

choices.text: Immediately revoke the app's OAuth consent for all 12 users via the Entra admin portal. Preserve audit logs of all app activity as evidence. Review 3 weeks of mailbox activity for the 3 affected executives — what was read and potentially exfiltrated? Treat as a confirmed email compromise and assess BEC risk.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. OAuth revocation immediately terminates the app's access without requiring user password changes. 3 weeks of executive mailbox access via a malicious app is a confirmed intelligence gathering operation — BEC assessment is mandatory. Evidence preservation supports potential legal action.

choices.text: Block the publisher domain at the firewall and monitor for further app activity.
choices.feedback: INSUFFICIENT. Firewall blocking of the publisher domain doesn't revoke the already-granted OAuth token — the app's API calls originate from Microsoft's infrastructure on behalf of the token, not from the publisher domain. OAuth revocation in Entra is the required action.

choices.text: Ask the 12 employees to manually revoke the app from their own account settings.
choices.feedback: TOO SLOW AND UNRELIABLE. User self-revocation requires each individual to navigate to their OAuth settings correctly. Admin-level revocation in Entra is instantaneous, centralized, and doesn't depend on 12 employees completing a manual step correctly.

injects.title: Email Data Staged for Exfiltration
injects.story: Audit logs show the malicious app read 4,200 emails from executive mailboxes and created a SharePoint folder '/shared/archive_backup_2024' containing copies of sensitive files including M&A documents, board meeting minutes, and client contracts. The SharePoint folder has an external sharing link created the same day.

mitre.technique: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
mitre.description: Attacker used OAuth-granted Files.ReadWrite.All permissions to stage sensitive documents in SharePoint and create an external sharing link for exfiltration — all via legitimate Microsoft API calls.

choices.text: Immediately disable the external SharePoint sharing link. Delete the attacker-created folder after preserving its contents as evidence. Engage Legal — M&A documents and board minutes in attacker hands is a material event requiring board notification and potential SEC disclosure assessment. Notify affected clients whose contract data was exposed.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. M&A document exposure may constitute material non-public information (MNPI) requiring SEC assessment. Board notification of a confirmed data theft of board materials is a governance obligation. Client contract exposure triggers individual client notification duties.

choices.text: Delete the SharePoint folder and revoke the sharing link to contain the exposure.
choices.feedback: TECHNICAL CONTAINMENT CORRECT but misses the regulatory and governance implications. M&A document and board minute theft requires Legal and Board notification — this is not just a technical incident to be quietly remediated.

choices.text: The sharing link was created but may not have been accessed yet — monitor before taking action.
choices.feedback: UNJUSTIFIED DELAY. A SharePoint external sharing link created by a confirmed malicious actor containing M&A documents and board minutes must be treated as accessed and exfiltrated — the burden of proof runs in the other direction. Disable immediately.

injects.title: OAuth Governance Framework
injects.story: Post-incident, your CISO must present an OAuth governance framework to prevent recurrence. The tenant currently has no admin consent policies, no app allow-listing, and no OAuth monitoring. What comprehensive framework do you recommend?

mitre.description: Post-OAuth-attack governance framework — implementing admin consent policies, app verification requirements, and continuous OAuth activity monitoring.

choices.text: Recommend: (1) Admin consent required for all apps requesting any permissions beyond basic sign-in. (2) App allow-list of approved apps maintained by IT. (3) Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps with OAuth app anomaly detection policies. (4) Quarterly review of all OAuth grants with automated revocation of unused grants. (5) User awareness training on OAuth consent risks.
choices.feedback: COMPREHENSIVE OAUTH GOVERNANCE. Admin consent policies are the primary preventive control. Allow-listing provides defense-in-depth. Defender for Cloud Apps provides continuous detection. Quarterly reviews prevent grant accumulation. User awareness addresses the social engineering component.

choices.text: Block all third-party app integrations with Microsoft 365 entirely.
choices.feedback: OVERCORRECTION. Blanket blocking of all third-party integrations is operationally disruptive and unlikely to survive business pressure. Risk-based admin consent policies achieve security without eliminating legitimate productivity tool integrations.

choices.text: Require employees to submit a helpdesk ticket before granting OAuth consent to any app.
choices.feedback: PROCESS WITHOUT ENFORCEMENT. Requiring a ticket doesn't technically prevent consent grants — employees can still grant consent in the browser without submitting a ticket. Admin consent policies in Entra are the technical enforcement control, not a process ticket requirement.

injects.title: SEC Disclosure Assessment
injects.story: Legal has determined that the exfiltrated M&A documents relate to a pending acquisition that has not been publicly announced. The documents contain material non-public information (MNPI). The SEC's 2023 cybersecurity disclosure rules require disclosure of material cybersecurity incidents within 4 business days of determining materiality. Is this a material incident requiring 8-K filing?

mitre.description: SEC Rule 13a-15 (2023) requires public companies to disclose material cybersecurity incidents within 4 business days of determining materiality — a new and consequential regulatory obligation.

choices.text: Engage SEC disclosure counsel immediately. The theft of MNPI related to a pending unannounced acquisition is very likely material — both for cybersecurity disclosure (theft of sensitive data) and potentially under insider trading regulations (MNPI in unauthorized hands). File Form 8-K within 4 business days of materiality determination if counsel concurs.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY CORRECT. The SEC's 2023 rules are clear: material cybersecurity incidents require 8-K disclosure within 4 business days of determining materiality. Stolen MNPI has dual implications — cybersecurity disclosure AND potential insider trading risk management. Specialized SEC counsel is required.

choices.text: Disclose in the next quarterly 10-Q filing — the 8-K requirement only applies to very large incidents.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY INCORRECT. The SEC's 2023 cybersecurity disclosure rules apply to all public companies and require 8-K filing within 4 business days of determining materiality — not quarterly disclosure. Delaying to the 10-Q for a material incident is a securities law violation.

choices.text: Treat as an internal incident only — public disclosure would alert the market to the pending acquisition.
choices.feedback: COMPLIANCE AVOIDANCE. SEC disclosure obligations exist precisely to protect investors. A cybersecurity incident involving MNPI cannot be withheld from disclosure to protect an undisclosed transaction — that reasoning itself raises additional securities law concerns. SEC counsel must make this determination, not internal preference.

scenario_meta.title: Operation Empty Vault
scenario_meta.subtitle: Smart Contract Exploit & Cryptocurrency Theft

injects.title: Smart Contract Audit Gap
injects.story: Your platform is preparing to launch a new DeFi lending feature with $50M in customer funds. An external security firm recommends a smart contract audit before launch. Engineering says the code was internally reviewed and the launch date cannot slip. The audit would take 3 weeks. Your CISO escalates to you. What is your recommendation?

mitre.description: Smart contract vulnerabilities are immutable once deployed — an unaudited contract managing $50M creates permanent, exploitable attack surface that a professional audit would identify before launch.

choices.text: Delay launch until the external audit is complete. $50M in customer funds on an unaudited smart contract is an unacceptable risk. The reputational and financial cost of a launch delay is orders of magnitude less than a smart contract exploit. Document the decision and the engineering pushback for Board awareness.
choices.feedback: CORRECT. Smart contract code is immutable once deployed — bugs cannot be patched, only worked around via complex migration. Multiple high-profile DeFi exploits ($600M+ losses industry-wide) have followed launches without independent audits. The delay cost is negligible vs. exploit risk.

choices.text: Launch with a $5M TVL cap until the audit completes, then increase to full capacity.
choices.feedback: REASONABLE RISK MITIGATION. Capping TVL limits financial exposure during the pre-audit window. This is a defensible middle ground if the launch delay is genuinely impossible, but the cap must be enforced technically, not just as a policy.

choices.text: Launch on schedule — the internal review was thorough and the team is confident in the code.
choices.feedback: UNACCEPTABLE RISK ACCEPTANCE. Internal code review and professional smart contract auditing are not equivalent. Professional auditors find classes of vulnerabilities (reentrancy, oracle manipulation, integer overflow) that internal reviewers systematically miss. 'Confident in the code' is the last statement made before most DeFi exploits.

injects.title: Flash Loan Attack Detected
injects.story: Your on-chain monitoring alerts fire: an attacker used a $40M flash loan to manipulate the price oracle in your lending contract, then borrowed against artificially inflated collateral, draining $28M in customer funds across 47 transactions in under 3 minutes. The transactions are visible on-chain. The attacker's wallet address is known. Funds are moving. What do you do?

mitre.description: Flash loan attack exploiting a price oracle manipulation vulnerability in a smart contract — a common DeFi attack pattern that executes entirely on-chain in a single atomic transaction.

choices.text: Immediately pause the smart contract (if a pause function exists). Alert blockchain analytics firms (Chainalysis, TRM Labs) with the attacker wallet address for real-time tracing. Notify all major exchanges to flag the address. Contact the FBI Virtual Assets Unit. Issue an immediate public statement — on-chain transparency means customers already know.
choices.feedback: CORRECT CRYPTO-NATIVE RESPONSE. Smart contract pause functions stop ongoing exploitation. Blockchain analytics firms can trace fund flows in real time as the attacker moves funds through mixers or bridges. Exchange flagging occasionally results in frozen funds. On-chain transparency makes immediate public disclosure both necessary and expected in the crypto community.

choices.text: Wait for the transactions to settle and do a post-mortem before taking any action.
choices.feedback: FATAL DELAY. Flash loan attacks complete in one block (~12 seconds on Ethereum). Waiting means all funds are already moved. The window for contract pausing, exchange alerting, and fund tracing is measured in minutes, not hours. Every second of inaction reduces recovery probability.

choices.text: Pause the smart contract and wait before making any public statement to assess the full scope.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL. Pausing the contract is correct. However, delaying the public statement in a DeFi context is counterproductive — the exploit is already visible on-chain to all blockchain analytics tools and crypto Twitter. Silence while funds are draining is perceived as hiding information and causes additional reputational damage.

injects.title: On-Chain Negotiation Attempt
injects.story: Blockchain analytics confirms $18M of the stolen $28M has moved to a Tornado Cash mixer and is unrecoverable. $10M remains in the attacker's wallet, unmoved. Some DeFi projects have successfully negotiated directly with attackers via on-chain messages (embedding text in transactions), offering to let the attacker keep 10% as a bug bounty in exchange for returning 90%. Should you attempt this?

mitre.description: Post-exploit fund recovery negotiation via on-chain messaging — an unconventional but occasionally successful DeFi-specific recovery tactic that has legal and regulatory implications.

choices.text: Consult legal counsel before any on-chain negotiation. An offer of 10% retention may constitute payment to a criminal and could violate OFAC sanctions if the attacker is a designated entity. If counsel clears it, a time-boxed on-chain offer for the $10M in the attacker's wallet is worth attempting — several DeFi projects have recovered funds this way.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY CORRECT PROCESS. On-chain negotiation has precedent in DeFi recovery (e.g., Euler Finance recovered $197M this way in 2023). However, OFAC sanctions screening of the attacker address is mandatory before any offer — paying a sanctioned entity carries $20M+ fines regardless of recovery intent.

choices.text: Immediately send an on-chain message offering 10% retention without legal review.
choices.feedback: SANCTIONS RISK. Unilateral on-chain negotiation without OFAC screening first is a compliance risk. If the attacker address is linked to a sanctioned entity (DPRK Lazarus Group accounts have been flagged in DeFi exploits), the offer itself may constitute a sanctions violation.

choices.text: Do not negotiate with criminals under any circumstances — report to FBI only.
choices.feedback: FORFEITS RECOVERABLE FUNDS WITHOUT JUSTIFICATION. Refusing all negotiation for the $10M sitting unmoved in the attacker's wallet — without even screening for OFAC issues and consulting legal counsel — abandons a legal recovery avenue that DeFi precedent (Euler Finance 2023: $197M recovered) supports. FBI reporting is mandatory and correct, but it does not preclude simultaneous legal negotiation for the uninstructed funds. Absolute refusal without legal review is a governance failure, not an ethical stance.

injects.title: Customer Restitution Decision
injects.story: Total recovered: $10M via negotiation. Total loss: $18M (in mixer, unrecoverable). 2,400 customers lost funds ranging from $500 to $200,000. Your company has $35M in reserves. Legal has reviewed: your Terms of Service disclaim liability for smart contract exploits. Engineering has patched the oracle vulnerability. Do you compensate customers?

mitre.description: Post-exploit restitution decision — balancing legal protections from Terms of Service against customer duty of care, regulatory expectations, and long-term platform trust.

choices.text: Fully compensate all 2,400 customers from reserves. While the ToS may provide legal protection, launching an unaudited contract with customer funds creates a compelling duty of care argument. Full restitution preserves customer trust, avoids class action litigation, and demonstrates platform integrity — all of which have greater long-term value than $18M in reserves.
choices.feedback: STRATEGICALLY AND ETHICALLY CORRECT. ToS protections are frequently successfully challenged in class actions for crypto exploits. Full restitution eliminates litigation risk, preserves the customer base, and is the precedent set by most well-regarded crypto platforms after major exploits (Binance, Bitfinex). The $18M cost is recoverable; the platform reputation may not be.

choices.text: Offer 50% restitution as a goodwill gesture, citing the ToS limitation of liability.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL MITIGATION. 50% restitution reduces financial exposure while demonstrating good faith. However, partially compensated customers are more likely to join class actions than fully compensated ones — the legal risk savings may be offset by litigation costs.

choices.text: Rely on the ToS and offer no restitution — customers accepted the risk of smart contract use.
choices.feedback: SHORT-TERM LEGAL, LONG-TERM CATASTROPHIC. ToS disclaimers do not reliably protect platforms from consumer fraud claims in US or EU courts, particularly when the exploit resulted from the platform's own failure to conduct an independent audit. Class action exposure, regulatory scrutiny, and platform abandonment are the likely outcomes.

injects.title: FinCEN & SEC Regulatory Assessment
injects.story: Your platform is registered as a Money Services Business (MSB) with FinCEN and is evaluating whether it qualifies as an exchange under SEC jurisdiction (pending regulatory clarity). FinCEN has inquired about the exploit given your MSB registration. The $28M theft involved customer funds. What are your regulatory obligations?

mitre.description: Post-exploit regulatory obligations for a registered MSB — FinCEN SAR filing, BSA compliance assessment, and SEC disclosure evaluation in the evolving crypto regulatory landscape.

choices.text: File a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) with FinCEN within 30 days — the exploit involves theft of funds from your MSB and the attacker's wallet address is a known suspicious entity. Engage crypto-specialized regulatory counsel for SEC disclosure assessment. Proactively brief FinCEN on your response and remediation steps.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY CORRECT FOR REGISTERED MSBs. FinCEN SAR obligations apply to MSBs for transactions involving suspected criminal activity — a $28M smart contract exploit clearly qualifies. Proactive FinCEN engagement demonstrates BSA compliance good faith. SEC assessment is mandatory given evolving crypto regulatory landscape.

choices.text: The exploit was on-chain and publicly visible — no regulatory reporting is needed since there is no concealment.
choices.feedback: LEGALLY INCORRECT. FinCEN SAR obligations are not contingent on concealment — they apply to suspected criminal activity involving your MSB regardless of on-chain public visibility. On-chain transparency does not substitute for regulatory reporting obligations.

choices.text: File the SAR but do not engage with SEC given the uncertainty about crypto regulatory jurisdiction.
choices.feedback: PARTIAL. SAR filing is correct. However, waiting for regulatory clarity before proactively assessing SEC obligations is a risk — if the SEC determines your platform qualifies as an exchange, the $28M incident is a material cybersecurity event requiring disclosure. Proactive counsel engagement is better than reactive compliance.
